We have established a principle that ensures the descent of special 0-cycles in abelian schemes over rings of integers. This established principle enables the verification of Hachim's conjecture for abelian schemes of dimension 2 and an infinite number of prime powers.

Pulsars are highly magnetized and rapidly spinning neutron stars, which have been found to produce various types of high-energy emissions across the electromagnetic spectrum. Specifically, some pulsars emit gamma-ray radiation via pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe), a phenomenon where high-energy particles are accelerated by the interaction between the pulsar wind and its surrounding interstellar medium. This phenomenon is often characterized by non-thermal radiation. This review will examine the non-thermal gamma-ray emissions produced by PWNe, focusing on the current understanding of these processes and the role of hadronic interactions in producing these emissions. We will also discuss the challenges in detecting and measuring the non-thermal emission from these sources.

We examine the long-term behavior – specifically the global attractors – of solutions to a specific class of high-dimensional reaction-diffusion equations, which have nonlinear terms that are homogeneous and high-order, and operate within a bounded domain, under the conditions that the initial data belong to a suitable Sobolev space and with emphasis on the influence of diffusion coefficients on the system's behavior.

The discovery of Ultra-compact dwarf galaxies (UCDs) and Globular Clusters (GCs) around galaxies is crucial for studying dark matter and dark matter halos. A recent study has identified 13 Ultra-massive Galaxies (UMGs) and 12 Ultra-compact Dwarf Galaxies (UCDc) in the Abell 96 galaxy cluster. By analyzing the velocity dispersions of these galaxies, researchers found that 3 of the UMGs and 2 of the UCDc are potentially hosted by dark matter halos. The findings of this study are consistent with previous research, indicating that UMGs and UCDc are found in similar proportions in both local and more distant galaxy clusters.

The widespread adoption of Recommender Systems across various online applications has led to a competitive landscape where only those that excel in performance quality remain in demand. In this context, the pursuit of optimal Recommender System performance has become an increasingly difficult challenge to overcome. In this research paper, we examine the obstacles that have been identified in the development of advanced RS methods, and we present a comprehensive survey of the most effective approaches to date. Specifically, we delve into the realms of collaborative filtering, content-based recommender systems, and hybrid methods, and we also explore advanced techniques in modeling user and item embeddings. Ultimately, the goal of this study is to provide a thorough understanding of the most effective methods for generating high-performance RS recommendations.

This article examines the asymptotic behavior of S\"urenhagen's test when applied to heavy-tailed distributions. The commonly held assumption in statistical software that normality applies is frequently violated, leading to substantial Type I errors. To mitigate this issue, various alternative tests have been developed, but their asymptotic behavior under heavy-tailed distributions has not been extensively studied. The article derives the asymptotic distribution of S\"urenhagen's test as the sample size approaches infinity under specific conditions for symmetric heavy-tailed distributions. Two cases are considered: when the fourth moment of the distribution is finite and when the moment is infinite. In the finite moment case, the distribution is a function of the sample mean's asymptotic variance, whereas in the infinite moment case, the distribution is a function of a more general variance. The results are demonstrated through Monte Carlo simulations using a range of heavy-tailed distributions.

A novel approach to developing closed-loop Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) has been proposed, utilizing artificial neural networks and multivariate EEG features. Our model enables near real-time classification of EEG signals to steer robotic arms in 3D space. A study demonstrated the effectiveness of this closed-loop BCI in enhancing user performance and tests its application in assisting individuals with paralysis. A key aspect of this project is the creation of an original dataset comprising two tasks performed by a 3D robotic arm controlled through EEG signals. This dataset is divided into training and testing sets, showcasing the primary challenge faced in this domain - transferring results from the training to the testing phase. To address this, we employed a technique called early-exiting, combining feature learning and ensemble learning to enhance accuracy. A specific implementation of this model, called CEFL-MLP, achieved notable outcomes in this research.

We've developed a method to numerically calculate the spatial correlation function of any light, single-trace operator in a four-dimensional conformal field theory, up to a certain order in perturbation. This method involves adjusting the conformal transformation of the operator, which changes its UV behavior. We then use a perturbative expansion of the modified conformal transformation in terms of the conformal operator, and match the expansion with the operator's UV behavior. We found that the two-point function can be expressed as a series of conformal blocks with coefficients determined by the operator's UV expansion, and that higher-order terms in the series can be calculated using a perturbative expansion of the operator product in terms of the block coefficients. We successfully calculated the third-order spatial correlation function of the Konishi operator in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory.

Due to a severe shortage of compatible donors, patients requiring kidney transplants are often transplanted with incompatible donors. This incompatible transplant may lead to the body rejecting the new kidney, causing the patient to return to dialysis until a compatible donor is found. Researchers have been exploring a method to accelerate the process of finding a compatible donor through genetic modification, but this approach remains in its early stages and is not without ethical concerns. To address this issue, we aim to develop a system that predicts the likelihood of successful organ transplantation from incompatible donors. By analyzing the genetic profiles of donors and recipients, we can identify the genetic variations that contribute to successful transplants. We have developed a machine learning model that can predict the success rate of kidney transplants in patients with incompatible donors. This model, trained on genetic data, demonstrates a significant predictive capability, suggesting that genetic factors play a crucial role in successful transplantations.

This study examines the predictive accuracy of Hidden Markov Models (HMM) and Long Short-Term Memory Models (LSTM) when used to identify the reasons for a customer leaving based on contact data. Both models were compared in terms of their ability to accurately predict customer contact behavior and the underlying reasons for their decisions. The research found that the choice of model does not significantly impact the predictive accuracy, but the HMM performs better when the data is noisy, whereas the LSTM outperforms when the data is clean.

This research focuses on generalizing the criteria for the boundedness and compactness of Volterra integral operators in the variable exponent Lebesgue spaces, by examining generalized versions of these operators. Initially, we establish the boundedness and compactness of generalized Volterra integral operators in LEspX_lp, where X is a domain in R^n with n being greater than or equal to three, and p varies between one and infinity. Subsequently, we analyze these operators in the space of homogeneous norms, denoted as hom_lp[μ]_X, which is a sub-space of LEspX_p.

Experience management, encompassing various industries such as entertainment and healthcare, heavily relies on capturing and understanding user behavior patterns. The application of multi-task modeling in experience management has gained significant traction due to its ability to integrate diverse data types and identify individualized user preferences. However, current state-of-the-art models fail to effectively incorporate temporal dependencies within their frameworks. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel approach, Temporal Experience Modeling (TEM), which leverages a graph-based neural network to seamlessly integrate temporal sequences and user preferences. Our proposed model is capable of efficiently learning from sequential data and adapting to various preference learning techniques, and we have successfully demonstrated its efficacy through extensive experiments on four publicly available datasets. Notably, TEM has achieved a remarkable 2.5% increase in NDCR compared to the existing state-of-the-art models.

In today's digital world, open data drives innovation and progress in various fields, including high energy physics. As researchers, we have a unique opportunity to push forward open data adoption and leverage its benefits in creating new forms of physics research and collaborating with other disciplines. This article highlights the current advancements and open data initiatives within high energy physics as well as the challenges that need addressing. It also touches on the potential pathways to fully realizing open data in this area of research and outlines the role of software and the contributions that the Software as a Service model can provide in achieving this goal.

We have developed a novel approach for separating the components of a Richelot isogeny, which enables us to create a pair of curves alongside an isogeny with a composite Richelot isogeny between them. This method can be applied to any pair of curves that have a Richelot isogeny between them, and we demonstrate its utility by generalizing Richelot curves and isogeny graphs for composite pairs, as well as providing an algorithm to compute richelotized Weierstrass curves via surface cover methods.

Recent discoveries of hot subdwarfs have reignited interest in these enigmatic stars. A comprehensive investigation into the relationship between hot subdwarfs and the local magnetic field is long overdue. To this end, a team of researchers conducted an exhaustive examination of the 1,000 brightest hot subdwarfs in the vicinity of the Milky Way. By combining publicly available polarization data with a refined analysis of the Galactic structure, they were able to establish precise upper and lower limits on the magnetic properties of these stars. Their findings suggest that hot subdwarfs are more likely to be magnetized than previously thought, with a possible magnetic fraction ranging from 0.1 to 0.9. A substantial portion of these magnetized hot subdwarfs reside in the Galactic bar. Further research is needed to fully understand the origins of the magnetic hot subdwarfs, but one theory is that they are formed through the interaction between the local magnetic field and the expanding interstellar medium.

In many fields, including statistics, machine learning, and related disciplines, we encounter positive semi-definite matrices that are often challenging to estimate due to their complex nature. This paper focuses on a specific group of positive semi-definite matrices, namely those that can be expressed as a convex combination of specific rank-one matrices. We develop an innovative method to estimate these combined matrices using only sample data that are moment-equivalent and without requiring any additional information. This method is rooted in a geometrically-inspired estimation strategy, enabling us to establish a minimal sample requirement to ensure the accuracy of our estimates. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our approach in two critical contexts: (i) the estimation of covariance matrices with unknown correlation coefficients, and (ii) the identification of influential data points within large datasets.

Wikipedia's page content is encoded in the Wikitext markup language, which is difficult to analyze directly. Instead, the article's actual content is contained within HTML equivalents of individual Wikipedia pages. Utilizing these HTML pages offers numerous benefits, as multiple Wikipedia editors can monitor and modify pages in real-time, allowing for the visualization of dynamic content that wouldn't be evident in Wikitext. Our study presents an automated method for converting article sections in Wikitext to HTML and transferring multimedia elements from article templates to their corresponding sections.

A theoretical model has been developed to describe the complex dynamics of macroscopic polarization in a specific type of bilayer system, comprising a superposition of two distinct layers with different properties, one of which is twisted at a specific angle relative to the other. This model incorporates both electrical and mechanical influences, enabling it to accurately simulate the behavior of these systems in the presence of various distortions. By applying this model to a specific type of twisted bilayer composed of two hexagonal boron nitride layers, the model reveals that the observed dynamics of this system can be accurately reproduced, provided that the two materials exhibit identical properties except for their orientation. This study demonstrates that the twisting of these layers gives rise to distinct polarization components, which are a consequence of symmetry breaking rather than a response to the applied voltage or mechanical strain. Importantly, the model shows that the observed behavior of this system is a consequence of a specific type of mechanical distortion that arises from the twisting of the layers, which is a unique feature of this type of system.

The universe's curvature is a crucial aspect of its structure that can be precisely quantified by combining data from various cosmic probes, including galaxy surveys, CMB analysis, and supernova observations. In this study, we employed a model that simultaneously examines the universe's evolution, curvature, and the growth of structure, utilizing a multi-probe analysis with BOSS galaxy data, SPT-3G data, and Pantheon supernova compilations. Our findings indicate that the universe's curvature is constrained at $\Omega_k=0.0385\pm 0.0193$ or $\Omega_k=-0.0074\pm 0.0113$ at 68% confidence, depending on the assumed equation of state of dark energy. Notably, the universe's curvature is consistent with flatness, but the results lack statistical significance. Our analysis also reveals that the universe's evolution is consistent with a $\Lambda$CDM model, and the curvature parameter is highly correlated with the dark energy equation of state.

The movement of particles within a specific environment, such as colloids in liquid crystals, is influenced by unique energy maps that are specific to the system. Research on the energy maps of these environments has been conducted using optical methods that measure how particles move when subjected to external forces. A theoretical model based on a mean field approach has been developed to describe these energy maps in terms of a specific mathematical function, allowing for the prediction of how particles behave in different situations. Our research provides a detailed analysis of how this function affects the way particles behave and presents a new method for calculating the function in different situations. Our findings were tested and confirmed by comparing them to real-life observations of how particles move in different situations, demonstrating that our model is a reliable predictor of particle behavior.

To examine how gravity affects an asteroid's surface, researchers used numerical models to analyze a fictional asteroid experiencing a close approach by Earth, focusing on how its shape and size influence the outcomes. They discovered that the elongation of the asteroid and its size have a significant impact on the gravitational forces acting upon its surface, particularly in scenarios where the asteroid experiences a substantial rotation due to the planetary encounter. In these scenarios, variations in the asteroid's surface slope are found to be directly related to its shape factor and size, but dependent in a complex manner on the parameters of the encounter. In contrast, the surface stress during a rotation-induced gravitational attraction exhibits a more predictable relationship with the asteroid's shape and size, being directly related to both factors but inversely related to the speed of the encounter.

Complex biological systems exhibit spontaneous changes in structure that play a key role in their function and organization. A new theoretical model has been developed to describe these transitions between different structures at a molecular level. By using this model to analyze data from simulations and experiments, it has been possible to quantify the nature of these transitions and their stable forms. The model also provides insight into how these transitions occur and the different pathways they can take. A further development of the model has allowed for the prediction of molecular structures based on experimental data, with potential applications in understanding the dynamics of biological systems without the need for complex simulations.

The causes behind the multiwavelength variability in high-energy gamma-ray sources are still not fully understood. Gamma-ray bursts and active galactic nuclei exhibit similar characteristics, but they have distinct time patterns. A key factor lies in the role of particle acceleration mechanisms, particularly in the high-energy radiation of jet sources. By analyzing the polarization of their radiation, scientists hope to gain insight into the source's characteristics and polarization properties. This review discusses the current state of research on polarisation measurements in high-energy gamma-ray sources, including the results of recent polarimetric studies. It also examines the challenges associated with such measurements and discusses the potential for future polarimetric missions, particularly in the context of the Cherenkov Telescope Array.

We've developed a model that explains how the ice thickness distribution $g(h)$ changes over time. This model is based on the ice thickness $h$ being influenced by the ice's age $t$, which is the amount of time since it froze. The distribution $g(h)$ can be expressed as a function of $t$, leading to the equation $g(h,t) = S(t)h^n$, where $n$ is the ice thickness exponent and $S(t)$ is the ice age probability density function. As the ice thins, the ice thickness exponent $n$ decreases, leading to the ice's elongation and eventual breakup. Our model predicts that the ice's elongation will be more pronounced in the ice age's initial stages, leading to the ice's breakup at a faster rate than previously thought. This model can be used to simulate the ice's breakup process, where the ice age $t$ is updated in increments of $\Delta t$ and the ice's elongation is calculated using the difference between the current ice thickness exponent $n$ and the ice's elongation at its initial state.

In this study, finding all the generalized Weierstrass semigroups associated with points on algebraic curves, as well as determining the topology of curves with specific embedded projective algebraic varieties, are explored.

Over the past few years, significant advancements in singing voice synthesis have been made, with numerous cutting-edge techniques being developed. This survey paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of machine learning-based singing voice synthesis, offering a thorough examination of the most effective approaches and a comprehensive summary of the field. The paper is divided into four key sections: (1) overview of the deep learning techniques used for SVS; (2) detailed analysis of the most widely used architectures for synthesizing raw audio, spectral features, and mel-spectra; (3) discussion of the most effective loss functions and training procedures; and (4) discussion of the evaluation metrics and the current state of research. Furthermore, various applications of SVS are explored, including its potential for assisting professional singers, creating virtual singing assistants, and developing more accurate singing voice synthesis models.

The absence of extensive, expertly labeled bird audio data has significantly hindered the development of effective detection and identification algorithms for birds. To address this challenge, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of fully annotated bird recordings. This new dataset, known as BirdsongNet, contains 4153 unique bird species and encompasses a wide variety of bird species, recording locations, and acoustic environments. We have employed a large convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify bird species based solely on their vocal sounds. This study presents an in-depth analysis of the BirdsongNet dataset, utilizing a CNN-based approach to classify bird species based on their vocal sounds. We have also released the BirdsongNet dataset, which can be found on the GitHub platform under the user 'xianjushv'.

We introduce a novel event camera calibration method utilizing a neural network for image reconstruction. By leveraging the event camera's internal clock, we derive initial intrinsic images and then use a neural network to construct image frames from these initial images. This allows us to calibrate camera parameters by processing image sequences of static scenes captured with the events. The network's effectiveness is further enhanced by the integration of a stereo module, which enables us to accurately determine camera position and orientation. Experimentally, our proposed approach outperforms existing methods in both event-based image construction and camera calibration tasks.

Graph learning involves working with data represented as complex networks, known as graphs, which are fundamentally different from traditional tabular data structures. This unique graph representation often mirrors underlying patterns and relationships within the data, but can also significantly hinder the efficiency of traditional machine learning algorithms. This paper provides an in-depth exploration of graph data properties and offers practical guidance on effectively handling and learning from such graph-based datasets. Additionally, we examine the key differences between tabular and graph data, and outline the specific design requirements and challenges associated with machine learning models that operate on graph data.

We examine the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on a specific class of del Pezzo surfaces, known as weak del Pezzo surfaces. This type of del Pezzo surface is characterized by having a relatively small Picard number of two and a smooth canonical model. Our study involves the analysis of exceptional objects within this category and their connections to a specific type of mutation on the dual root system. Furthermore, we establish that these objects possess the property of being $t$-tilting for all values of $t$ in a specific set of positive roots. This finding enables us to prove that these objects, when related through derived equivalences, can be directly connected to a sequence of successively mutated roots. Ultimately, we demonstrate that these derived equivalences can be integrated into a larger structure known as a "derived cluster category".

A novel image-guided robotic surgery system is introduced for retinal procedures. Building on the Versatile Robot System, the guidance and control features are enhanced to accommodate an extended range of motion. The system's performance is evaluated through simulation-driven research. A realistic virtual environment, the Virtual Retina Environment, is created and the robotic system is tested using real-world surgical data. The long-term objective is to develop an image-guided robotic surgery (IRGS) system for performing non-contacting surgical procedures such as panretinal photocoagulation.

This study introduces a family of polynomials, specifically $F$-polynomials, which are derived from the intersection coefficients of a generalized cluster algebra $A$. By utilizing these coefficients, we define the $F$-polynomials over the algebra $A$. The paper establishes that these coefficients adhere to a recursive relationship known as the mutation formula. Furthermore, we identify an explicit formula for the $F$-polynomials, which are specifically expressed as rational functions over $A$. The explicit formula is characterized by the structure of an updated cluster and an associated quiver containing a specific "source" node.

The concept of passwordless authentication has gained significant traction, with various experts predicting an imminent shift away from traditional password systems. However, we argue that a complete password abolition is not imminent in the foreseeable future. The main obstacles to this transition include the widespread use of passwords and the need for more effective and widely accepted alternative forms of authentication. The push for passwordlessness is often driven by the tech industry without considering the needs and infrastructure of their users. Moreover, there is ongoing debate and uncertainty about how to replace traditional passwords and the potential costs associated with their replacement.

A major constraint of discrete lattice models lies in their inability to incorporate compact momentum within a continuous momentum space, necessitating a novel approach. We present a new method that involves utilizing a discrete lattice not only for the spatial arrangement of particles but also for their momentum distribution, effectively eliminating the need for compactness. This breakthrough enables the attainment of a continuous momentum space, unencumbered by the constraints typically associated with it. This paper serves as an introductory foundation, providing a comprehensive overview of the underlying concepts, applications, and benefits of employing a lattice not only for momentum but also spatial distribution.

A widely adopted feature in online video platforms, autoplay, enables websites to display videos without user initiation. Although it increases engagement, autoplay significantly infringes upon users' discretion and overall wellbeing. This research examines the effects of autoplay on user behavior in mobile video applications and discovers that autoplay leads to a notable decrease in overall viewing time. Notably, even when users are exposed to videos through autoplay, they are less likely to engage with or seek out additional videos. Interestingly, users who are actively using the app simultaneously with the video loop experience prolonged viewing times compared to when they are passively exposed to videos. This study's findings suggest that while autoplay may enhance metrics like watch time, it comes at the expense of user agency and overall user experience.

Reactive Turing machines have been expanded to incorporate a self-organizing capability, enabling them to adjust their internal state and transition rules based on the intersection of their own behavior and environmental responses. This self-modification potential makes the concept of finitely executable behavior significant, as it can be executed using a limited number of resources, even in the presence of infinite input. Although the reaction mechanism's influence on finite executability remains unclear, it has been discovered that a behaviour is finitely executable if and only if it can be translated into Church's untyped lambda-calculus system. Consequently, the problem of determining the finitely executable elements of a reactive Turing machine's specification becomes a computationally complex issue, falling under the class of PSPACE-complete problems.

A combinatorial Gray code represents all feasible combinations of a specific type of object in such a way that transitioning from one object to the next one only involves a minimal alteration of the underlying structure. In this paper, we focus on a type of Gray code known as subword codes, specifically the subword gray code, to list all possible subwords of a given word. We present an algorithm that can generate the subword Gray code of a given word both quickly and in a way that only changes the word by a minimal number of operations. Additionally, we use this algorithm to develop an efficient method to remove words from a word set while keeping the set connected, specifically in cases where connectivity is determined by the subword relation.

The sPHENIX experiment at RHIC is designed to examine the fundamental structure of matter in high-energy collisions, leveraging a powerful detector and 220 TeV collisions to study particles, nuclei, and their interactions. The experiment's key objectives include understanding color and energy flow, investigating the behavior of small systems, and exploring the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. The following sections detail sPHENIX's hardware and design, highlighting its capabilities and system integration while highlighting remaining technical challenges.

This study introduces an efficient approach for minimizing the computational cost of solving partial differential equations that involve time-dependent and spatially deforming domains. Our strategy, known as space-time discretization with dual schwarz methods, is designed to handle complex interactions between the domain boundaries and the differential equation's smooth solution. Our implementation, which involves discretizing space-time slabs with higher-order finite elements, also includes a boundary averaging technique to ensure accurate representation of the boundary conditions. Our dual schwarz method, which applies finite elements to a coarse grid, is shown to provide a convenient and efficient way to solve problems with changing domains, as demonstrated by numerical experiments on both stationary and time-dependent Poisson problems in moving domains. Our results show that the proposed method maintains the optimal convergence rate of the finite element method, even when the domain boundaries are closely located, which is facilitated by our boundary averaging technique.

In a recent paper, the concept of the circular flow index in signed graphs was introduced, representing a weighted combination of all possible cycles with alternating signs in the graph. Specifically, the circular flow index of a cycle itself within the graph is equivalent to its signature. Recent findings by Bogacz and Diaz, including a breakthrough theorem, have been restated and further extended by our research, which also confirms the existing results through a straightforward method. Moreover, we have derived a characterization of specific types of signed graphs characterized by circular flows of particular signs.

We investigate the Modular Subset Sum problem, defined as: given $n$ integers between $0$ and $m$, find a subset of integers $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ in $\mathbb{Z}_m$ whose sum equals $0 \bmod m$. Our research presents a Monte-Carlo randomized algorithm for this problem, achieving an $O(n \cdot m^{3/4} \cdot \log m \cdot \log \log m)$ time complexity. This is the first randomized algorithm for Modular Subset Sum with a sublinear time complexity. Additionally, we introduce a deterministic algorithm for Modular Subset Sum with a near-linear time complexity of $O(n \cdot m^{1/2})$.

Our team has conducted an investigation into the H-alpha emission of nearby M dwarf stars using the 2.1-meter Otto Struve Telescope at the McDonald Observatory. We have compiled a list of 407 stars with a distance of less than 25 parsecs from the General Catalogue of Stars and other nearby stars. We have obtained data for 345 of these stars using the DIS, and we have also included data from the literature for the remaining 62 stars. We have identified 444 H-alpha flares in our sample, and we have found that flaring stars are hotter and more luminous than average M dwarfs. We have also found that the flaring rate increases with stellar mass and luminosity, and we have identified a correlation between flare frequency and stellar age. Additionally, we have found that the flaring rate decreases with increasing mass for the lowest mass stars, and we have identified a correlation between flare frequency and surface gravity. We have also found that the flaring rate is higher for stars with lower rotation rates, and we have identified a correlation between flare frequency and rotation rate. We have also found that the flaring rate is higher for stars with lower magnetic field strengths, and we have identified a correlation between flare frequency and magnetic field strength.

During the development of Drosophila melanogaster, a significant number of hemocytes are formed in the body cavity, which will eventually lose their immune capabilities as adults approach. These cells, which serve as the insect's first line of defense, play a crucial role in the organism's development and function. Notably, a substantial portion of these cells are lost during the development stage of the organism, which poses a challenge for researchers attempting to study this process. In order to overcome this limitation, a novel method has been developed that allows researchers to observe and interact with these cells during the development and early adulthood stages of the organism, which will significantly facilitate research in the field of developmental immunology. This method utilizes a transgenic Drosophila line specifically engineered to produce a fluorescent marker in the cells, which are then isolated and studied using a unique procedure. This procedure involves treating the cells with a gentle detergent solution, which helps to preserve the cells' structure and prevent the disruption of the cells, allowing researchers to observe the cells' morphology and perform further analysis.

This study introduces a siamese network that pairs two autoencoders for non-audio speech training, operating under a contrastive learning framework. Unlike traditional siamese networks, which generate a dense similarity score, our approach uses contrastive loss to learn representations that differ significantly when a specific class is not present. Each autoencoder compresses input data into distinct feature sets, post-processed by a triplet loss function that aims to bring similar features together and separate dissimilar ones. Experimental results demonstrate that this method results in comparable word error rates for non-audio speech recognition when compared to conventional auto-encoder-based approaches.

The parton distribution functions (PDFs) of the valence quarks are determined through high-precision measurements of the JLab Hall C experiment's longitudinal cross section for single-pion production. By utilizing the single-spin asymmetry data from the scattering of polarized electrons against protons at a low momentum scale of about 1.6 GeV, the authors extract the valence quark distributions $u_v$, $d_v$, and $u_c-d_c$ in the new scaling variable $\xi_w$. This new variable effectively reduces the uncertainty of the gluon PDFs and enhances the separation of the valence and sea quark flavors. The resulting PDFs are then used to calculate the single-pion production cross section, which matches the measured data. Furthermore, the valence PDFs are used to calculate the proton's and the neutron's Drell-Yan asymmetry at a high momentum scale of 200 GeV, demonstrating good agreement with the T-PEPIII Drell-Yan data.

This study investigates the use of adaptive control in an input-constrained linear system. The control strategy is adjusted based on the output of a ratio that includes measurement noise. We identify conditions under which the adaptive control system forms a regular process, allowing us to apply linear stochastic process theory. Under normal conditions, these conditions lead to the control target converging to a steady state value. However, when outliers occur, the conditions ensure that the control system remains stable and resumes normal operation. We also develop a stabilizing control algorithm that meets these conditions and outperforms a baseline approach by reducing constraints. The performance of our method is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world data from a robotic arm.

A new theory, branching time active inference (BTAI), has been proposed to explain brain function in relation to an agent's concept of itself and its place in the world. This framework, rooted in the concept of possible worlds, models an agent's knowledge through a graph of distinct scenarios. This graph is seen as a way to encode an agent's beliefs in a way that is compatible with neural connections. This paper examines the implications of using a specific type of neural connection, known as sparse connectivity, in the context of BTAI. Using a mathematical model, we investigate the relationship between this type of neural connection and the properties of branching time, and show that it leads to a scenario where the brain is able to process information in a way that is consistent with this theory. This is shown through a model of a brain that is able to learn about its own knowledge, and show that it is able to infer its own knowledge, and we discuss the implications of this for a new model of the brain.

Researchers have used the relativistic viscous hydrodynamic model to study how a dense, nonlinear medium responds to a sudden change in baryon density, focusing on whether this change can occur at a constant speed. They found that in certain conditions, such as those seen in heavy ion collisions at the RHIC and LHC, a density pulse can move at a constant speed, with its speed determined solely by the initial state properties, independent of the medium's state.

This research delves into the characteristics of specific spaces within the Banach space framework, namely Eberlein-Grothendieck spaces. We have successfully proven that certain Tychonoff spaces, possessing specific properties, result in corresponding spaces of continuous functions that exhibit similar characteristics. We then demonstrate the Eberlein-Grothendieck nature of several first-countable, separable spaces, including those that are non-metrizable and do not support the countable network property. Our study also reveals that every closed subspace of L1[0,α] space belongs to the Eberlein-Grothendieck class when α equals 1 or 2, and we explore the Eberlein-Grothendieck status of specific spaces, including Q, 1<α<1+b and 1<β<1+b, where b>1.

This paper outlines a process to determine the required modifications to a given Hamiltonian system with a single variable, aimed at achieving isochronicity. The approach involves directly manipulating the frequency of the system, which is based on an unimportant constant and can be expressed in terms of the original Hamiltonian function. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the necessary adjustments can be made by adding a particular type of harmonic oscillation term. The process is also formalized to establish a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving the desired system dynamics.

A new technique for analyzing complex systems is presented, which utilizes a unique metric to identify patterns in behavior. This approach, known as the similarity signature curve, is applied to the Lorenz system and reveals a distinct pattern following initial chaos.

The LAN property has been proven for a specific functional central limit theorem associated with a class of functional data under a general statistical framework that includes observations from the solution to stochastic differential equations driven by L\'evy processes. The key concept is to establish a general LAN property for a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables, and then apply it to the LAN property in the context of functional central limit theorems.

This paper provides a detailed spectral study for a family of non-self-adjoint Laplacians on a flat vector bundle, specifically over compact hyperbolic surfaces, where we establish the high-frequency asymptotics based on the Hecke theory. The results include the counting function and the spectral asymptotics. Notably, the high-frequency asymptotics differ from those of self-adjoint Laplacians. Additionally, the spectral asymptotics are further analyzed and compared to the spectral mean of the Laplacian on the hyperbolic plane.

This paper proposes FNetAR, a novel algorithm for causal language modeling, built upon the FNet framework, incorporating AR residual connections to enhance self-attention performance and match or surpass the capabilities of the Transformer-XL baseline in few-shot word-level prediction tasks.

In this research, we investigate the behavior of an ideal fluid in an accelerated universe, with its evolution governed by a modified Friedmann-Robert-Walker metric. We examine the transition from a deceleration to an acceleration phase, and analyze the impact of various parameters on the present state of the universe. We also investigate the thermodynamic properties of the fluid in light of the second law of thermodynamics, and discuss the stability of the system in terms of its thermodynamic and kinetic stability. Furthermore, we determine the point at which the universe shifts from a deceleration to an acceleration phase, and investigate the conservation laws governing the fluid.

A groundbreaking approach to network service delivery, known as service function chaining (SFC), has the potential to significantly enhance network functionality. However, implementing SFC in networks with limited resources can lead to substantial increases in traffic, causing network congestion and negatively impacting Quality of Service (QoS). To mitigate this issue, we introduce a game theory-based framework that enables software-defined networks to efficiently manage traffic and maintain optimal QoS levels. By developing a Stackelberg game model that takes into account edge network limitations, this framework can effectively minimize traffic in network edge environments. To validate its performance, we conducted extensive simulations on various complex network scenarios.

In two-dimensional disordered superconductors, the phase transition between the diffusive thermal metal and topological superconductor states exhibits a unique critical behavior. Our study examines the interplay between these states and a clean 2D topological superconductor state in the presence of disorder, using an exactly solvable model. We analyze the interplay between the metal and topological superconductor phases near criticality, demonstrating a phase transition between the diffusive thermal metal and topological superconductor states. Our findings show that the transition is consistent with the Kibble-Zurek mechanism and the scaling theory of critical phenomena.

This study examines the interplay between manifestations of happiness on social media platforms and their correlation with self-reported depression in Instagram users. Using a dataset comprising 4,674,743 users and 7,821,537 posts across three months, we analyzed Instagram's visual content and the emotions it conveyed, as well as the posts users created directly from their mental health surveys. Our analysis reveals a striking contrast: users who reported high levels of depression posted significantly fewer posts that depicted happy emotions, even after adjusting for demographic variables. This inverse relationship between depression and the pursuit of happiness has important implications for our understanding of social media's role in both promoting and inadvertently perpetuating mental health issues.

A long-standing problem in astrophysics is identifying the composition and behavior of dark matter.  Various theoretical models such as WIMPs, sterile neutrinos, and axions have been proposed to explain these phenomena but have not been conclusively proven or disproven.  This article will examine the current state of research on dark matter especially focusing on its interactions with normal matter and its detectability by experimental methods.  Particular emphasis will be placed on a novel approach to dark matter detection that involves its self-conjugate nature interacting with normal matter in a way that leaves behind a distinctive signature on experimental data.  This approach has been found to explain the observed pattern in a specific type of experimental data and could potentially provide insights into the nature of dark matter if further data supports this theory.

Na4-δNiTeO6 is a unique compound featuring a four-fold nickel spin state, with a specific moment size and a magnetic structure consisting of a 4x4x4 columnar spinel. This compound's spin structure remains unchanged down to 1.8 K, with a magnetic moment size of 2.0 μB. The compound's behavior is influenced by a Te-Te-Te framework, with a planar framework of Na/Ni layers playing a key role in its spin structure. The compound's specific structure results in a unique magnetic property, with a specific field applied causing the spin structure to switch at 40 K.

The growing reliance on IoT networks as a powerful tool for data analysis has created a pressing need to develop a comprehensive trust framework that addresses the complexities of trust establishment in these environments. Given the dynamic nature of IoT networks and the uncertainty surrounding their data sources, it has become essential to incorporate methods for quantifying uncertainty and updating trust ratings based on reliable information. This research proposes a novel, Bayesian network-based framework that enables the measurement of data trustworthiness and node reliability in IoT networks. By leveraging Bayesian networks to represent data reliability and trust, this framework is able to incorporate uncertainty and integrate multiple trust sources. It also utilizes a directed graph to model trust establishment and evaluation, taking into account data reliability, node trust, and re-evaluation of trust ratings. To validate the efficacy of this framework, we have developed a case study centered on smart agriculture, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing trust models, using both synthetic and real-world data.

Cubic spline interpolation is a widely used method due to its ability to preserve linear and monotonic properties.
However, it often leads to the Gibbs phenomenon in irregular cases, which causes periodic interpolations to produce undesirable oscillations. 
To mitigate the Gibbs phenomenon, researchers have proposed various methods, such as the Lanczos kernel, which is particularly effective in producing smooth interpolations. 
This study focuses on combining cubic spline interpolation with the Lanczos kernel to produce high-quality results. 
The paper demonstrates the use of the Lanczos kernel in various scenarios, such as interpolating a single data point, applying cubic spline interpolation, and even using it to approximate a cubic spline's second derivative. 
Through a series of experiments, it is shown that the proposed method significantly reduces the Gibbs phenomenon while maintaining the monotonicity of the interpolations. 
The results also highlight the method's ability to produce high-quality results in practical scenarios, such as approximating a function's second derivative without violating monotonicity constraints.

This research examines four-dimensional Taub-NUT spacetime in Einstein-$\lambda$ theory, focusing on a non-minimally coupled scalar field. By analyzing the theory through a specific coordinate transformation, we arrive at a novel set of spacetimes. This study yields two key results: a family of four-dimensional black holes and two distinct cosmologies, which can be characterized by the presence or absence of scalar hairs. This work expands our understanding of non-minimal scalar hair through the Einstein-$\lambda$ coupling mechanism.

Accurate multimedia content annotation is crucial for effective Information Retrieval applications, but current annotation schemes are limited in addressing the complexity of real-world situations. Existing approaches focus on specific concepts like actions or objects, but neglect their interconnected nature. We propose a comprehensive annotation framework that integrates a range of domains, allowing for the flexible representation of human-centric activities in a dynamic environment. By merging probabilistic models, we develop a structured annotation system that can be efficiently computed from incomplete or uncertain information. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach in annotating complex scenes, even with incomplete or uncertain data, and demonstrate its ability to handle noisy labels and multiple annotations per location.

Theoretical research on the preservation of diversity in complex ecosystems has made considerable progress in recent years. Notably, theories such as the 'Darwinian Axiom' and the 'Molt and Grow' model have identified key mechanisms that support diversity - specifically, the creation of isolated areas where the less fit population thrives and the accumulation of individual traits through continuous growth and subsequent shedding. However, these models rely on the assumption that the population remains relatively constant, which is not applicable to many real-world examples. This paper aims to address this limitation by developing a new model that accounts for changing population sizes in ecosystems. By incorporating density regulation and demographic fluctuations, the research provides a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying processes governing diversity. The proposed model builds upon the 'Molt and Grow' framework and leverages the principles of branching random walks to analyze the impact of density regulation. The findings support the 'Molt and Grow' hypothesis and demonstrate that density regulation is a crucial factor in preserving diversity, particularly in the presence of demographic fluctuations. This research has significant implications for our understanding of the mechanisms maintaining diversity in various ecosystems, including certain types of plankton, frogs, and certain species of insects.

Network vulnerability analysis is a primary focus in graph theory, with researchers employing various methods to understand network resilience. A novel approach to assessing network vulnerability involves ranking nodes based on the size of information diffusion waves triggered by their removal. This phenomenon is known as an avalanche, which can be measured by the number of affected neighbors and the timeframes of the resulting cascades. To address this problem, we present efficient algorithms to calculate avalanche metrics in networks, highlighting their potential through case studies and discussing broader implications.

To assess deep understanding during text comprehension, we introduce a metric for evaluating the depth of knowledge in open-ended questions. Unlike existing methods, our metric directly assesses the depth of knowledge rather than the question's complexity or answer accuracy. Our approach involves creating a knowledge graph representing the text and evaluating questions in terms of the number of distinct nodes required to answer them. This knowledge graph is built through a series of text processing steps, where entities and concepts are extracted and then merged based on equivalence or subsumption. By calculating the logarithmic number of ancestors for each question, we obtain a logarithmic scale reflecting the depth of knowledge required. Our metric is validated through human annotations and experiments on several datasets.

The source-free time-domain scalar wave equation is discretized using finite differences both in space and time. To prevent spurious reflections in numerical solutions for wave propagation problems, absorbing boundary conditions such as perfectly matched layers (PML) are utilized. In this research, a novel approach to detect and remove PML-related numerical errors is introduced. By dividing the computational domain into two subdomains with separate PML conditions, a novel method is developed to validate numerical results. The proposed technique is supported by simulations of both wave sources within the computational domain and ground motion recordings from actual earthquakes.

Arrays of droplets, comprising air or water, are utilized in various fields, and their fluid-dynamic response can be manipulated by adjusting droplet size, velocity, spacing, or motion patterns. A novel approach of droplet arrays featuring droplets moving in tandem in both longitudinal and transverse directions is presented, and it leverages the interplay of these two motions to fine-tune their fluid-dynamic characteristics. The research focuses on an array of droplets experiencing Marangoni-Marangoni interactions, and it demonstrates that by synchronizing droplet motion in both directions, flow behavior can be modulated and optimized, and specific geometrical parameters can be adjusted to achieve desired outcomes.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a highly connected system, enabling the interaction of physical and digital components. The diversity of IoT applications, such as smart grids and self-driving vehicles, necessitates reliable communication quality. Quality of Service (QoS) is a critical factor in IoT applications, particularly in scenarios where network resources are limited. This paper examines the QoS requirements for IoT, including the challenges faced in traffic management and the impact of network protocols on resource allocation. To address these issues, we propose a novel traffic management approach and evaluate the influence of Distributed-Layer-2 Switching (DLS) and Virtual Switching (VS) on network performance.

This research introduces a new method of estimating a matrix that lies between two other matrices, utilizing a vector-valued distance metric. Our approach draws inspiration from the geometric Mean Isotropic Logarithmic (IMiLOG) distance, a non-Euclidean metric applicable to the space of symmetric positive definite matrices, and is specifically tailored for that space. Our estimation technique is shown to be efficient, and we demonstrate its real-world effectiveness in analyzing the relationships between pairs of symmetric positive definite matrices, particularly within the fields of statistics, machine learning, and robotics.

To combat climate change, the European Union has set a goal of achieving 100% renewable energy usage, primarily through the accelerated expansion of wind power.  This shift is expected to lead to fluctuations in energy supply, but an interconnected network of hydrogen systems can mitigate these variations by storing excess energy.  This study examines the potential of a large-scale hydrogen grid stretching from Scandinavia to Portugal, linking together several key regions, including the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and the Iberian Peninsula, to maintain a consistent power supply.  By modeling the system and analyzing multiple scenarios, the study demonstrates the capacity of a hydrogen-based power network to balance out fluctuations in renewable energy production and ensure a reliable energy supply.  Specifically, a high-resolution power flow model of the European grid, combined with an optimized hydrogen supply chain, reveals that a large-scale hydrogen grid can effectively stabilize the energy mix.  This is particularly true for periods of high energy demand, such as winter afternoons, when renewable energy production often fails to meet demand, but the system is able to compensate by releasing stored hydrogen.  Ultimately, the study's findings suggest that a large-scale hydrogen grid can play a crucial role in maintaining a balanced and reliable energy supply in a future European renewable energy market.

Researchers have developed a new method to determine the orientation of horizontal magnetic fields beneath the Earth's surface by analyzing how seismic waves behave in response to changing gravitational forces. This technique utilizes travel time anisotropy measurements to identify the direction of subsurface magnetic fields, with results indicating a strong correlation with rapid ground deformation caused by removal of heavy iron deposits. The study found that subsurface magnetic fields at depths of around 3 kilometers follow the direction of the Earth's ancient magnetic field as recorded in and around the Earth's crust. The new method has the potential to identify subsurface magnetic fields in areas where ancient magnetic fields are difficult to reconstruct and can be applied to a wide range of regions, including areas with significant volcanic activity.

Generating squeezed light is crucial for advancing quantum sensing and information processing capabilities. By producing such light, researchers can develop more precise instruments for detecting minute changes and perform quantum computations with enhanced accuracy. In particular, this can be achieved by engineering optical parametric oscillators (OPOs) that produce not only classical but also quantum squeezed states. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of creating an integrated hybrid OPO that combines a quantum cascade laser as the gain medium and a ring resonator for confinement, all within a single chip. By leveraging the unique properties of this hybrid device, such as its ability to produce photons in arrays and our proposed resonator design, we show that the system can efficiently produce squeezed light at room temperature. By analyzing the potential sources of quantum noise in this OPO, such as its pump noise and amplified spontaneous emission, and developing strategies to mitigate them, we find that the hybrid device is capable of producing high-quality squeezed states.

This paper examines the development of a time-optimization strategy for a drone with limited rotation and acceleration capabilities, working under the influence of wind and gust forces. It outlines a method to calculate the minimum-time control input necessary for the drone to transition between two distinct targets. Additionally, the manuscript discusses the computation of the minimum-time control input necessary for the drone to track a dynamic target with changing location, as well as presents numerical case studies to support the derived theoretical findings.

This research outlines the underlying structure of a specific type of code called the additive conjugacy code, created using a group action on finite fields. Specifically, we identify the conditions under which this code is equivalent to a linear, cyclic code constructed using a standard method.

The pursuit of an academic career in physics can be a challenging endeavor,
particularly for individuals seeking to secure positions at institutions that
primarily cater to undergraduate students or community-based learning.
Physics departments at these institutions often have limited resources and
research facilities, which can hinder their ability to provide opportunities for
faculty to engage in substantial research endeavors. Consequently, aspiring
physicists who are considering joining such institutions are in need of guidance
regarding the feasible paths for their professional development. This article aims
to provide an overview of the existing research networks and initiatives that support
physicists who hold positions at these institutions.

This study examines the polarization of W bosons from top quark decays, specifically those that result in a hadronic top quark decaying into a W boson and a hadronic B quark. The latter is identified through a multijet signature and large missing transverse momentum. The research utilizes a dataset of 32.9 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions collected by the CDF II detector at the Tevatron between 2001 and 2008. The analysis focuses on events with a high-energy lepton emitted from the W boson, along with several top quark kinematic variables, to distinguish between pure left-handed and right-handed W boson decays. The results indicate that the observed left-handed and right-handed fractions are 0.2155 and 0.1845, respectively, with an uncertainty of 0.0174 and 0.0125, respectively, allowing for an extraction of the left-right asymmetry of the top quark decay process. The findings are consistent with predictions from the Standard Model.

We investigate the decay of $B\to D\pi$ using a twist-2 and twist-3 parton distribution amplitude framework for the $D$-meson. By establishing a relationship between these amplitudes, we derive a concrete expression for the $D$-meson twist-2 amplitude in terms of its twist-3 counterpart. This relationship is essential for accurately calculating the $B\to D\pi$ decay rate and related decay processes. Furthermore, we calculate the partial Brans-Dijk-Kubis-Lee-Swanson partial width for $B\to D\pi$ using soft collinear factorization and our proposed relation between twist-2 and twist-3 distribution amplitudes.

This research investigates a power extension of hypergraphs, focusing on the eigenvalues of the signed adjacency matrix. A real-valued function is used to modify the adjacency matrix, resulting in the signed adjacency matrix. The eigenvalues of a signed subgraph are shown to be influenced by the eigenvalues of a power hypergraph, allowing the creation of these eigenvalues. A real-valued function is used to modify the adjacency matrix of a power hypergraph, enabling the derivation of a sufficient condition for the existence of such eigenvalues. The derived condition is more inclusive than existing results for specific power hypergraph exponents, including negative ones.

The deployment of mega-constellations in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) consisting of thousands of satellites poses significant challenges for their spatial management and tracking. In this context, we investigate the application of cooperative localization techniques to improve the tracking of LEO mega-constellations. Our research involves simulating a scenario of satellite formation and evaluating the localisation accuracy of a single satellite using cooperative methods, such as time-of-arrival and received signal strength indication, based on measurements from its peers. The results reveal that cooperative localization can achieve centimeter-level precision within a formation of 10 satellites. Furthermore, we examine the localisation metrics and trade-offs by varying the formation configuration, communication protocols, and cooperative aspects. The findings suggest that cooperative localization can be a viable solution for mega-constellations, particularly when traditional navigation systems are insufficient or impractical.

Theories on hot Jupiters' formation rely heavily on understanding their migration patterns.  Transit timing variation (TTV) analysis can provide insight into a planet's orbital evolution.  However, the method is often complicated due to the influence of other celestial bodies in the system.  Our study focuses on TTV measurements for KELT-9Ab, aiming to verify if the planet's orbit is being affected by the star's obliquity.  Our research involved analyzing all available transit data for the KELT-9 system and comparing it with general models of orbital precession.  Our findings show that the data do not align with the predicted patterns, but we were unable to determine the reason behind the discrepancy.  Our results also suggest that the planet's orbital evolution is unlikely to be driven by obliquity-induced migration.  Our conclusions are further supported by the influence of third-body effects, which are thought to be the primary cause of the observed TTV in the KELT-9 system.

A novel, advanced cosmic calorimeter known as ProtoDAME, is being developed for the DAME experiment at the University of Washington to improve its cosmic signal detection capabilities. This custom-made calorimeter, comprising 25 layers of ETL wave-shifting plates and scintillating crystals, is designed to enhance the experiment's sensitivity and accuracy in detecting and calibrating cosmic signals. By incorporating a unique feature, which allows the system to be easily reconfigured and adaptable, it can effectively differentiate between various types of cosmic signals and events. This adaptable design also enables the incorporation of multiple event trigger strategies, including self-contained configurations.

We demonstrate that on algebraic GKM manifolds, for two equivariant vector bundles with identical equivariant Chern classes, their characteristic classes are also identical, and they are uniquely determined by their equivariant Chern classes. Furthermore, we establish that the total space of one of these bundles can be mapped equivariantly onto the total space of the other.

We have developed a simplified proof of the prime number theorem that not only is it a more streamlined version of the original proof by Hadamard and Lagrange, but it also achieves this while significantly reducing the complexity of the analysis required. By replacing the regularity lemma with a more manageable upper bound, we are able to provide a proof that is more accessible to those interested in the fundamental aspects of number theory. The approach we have taken involves a more direct examination of prime numbers within an expanded arithmetic series, ultimately revealing that the distribution of primes can be understood through a straightforward examination of an infinite series.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and other progressive diseases, linear mixed mixed models for repeated measurements are commonly used. However, the use of categorical time can lead to biased estimates if the interval lengths vary among treatments. Researchers have proposed models with varying definitions of categorical time, yet no comprehensive comparison exists. This study examines the impact of different categorical time definitions on estimated treatment effects and power, utilizing both simulated and real data. The findings indicate that employing distinct definitions of categorical time can yield contrasting results. Consequently, the choice of definition is not merely a matter of convenience but has a significant bearing on potential treatment outcomes. For accurate and reliable results, models should be fitted with multiple definitions of categorical time.

We introduce an efficient crowdsourcing algorithm for routing large numbers of connected cars over long distances. Our proposed strategy divides the journey into two segments. First, it identifies the most popular route among cars traveling in similar directions using a basic voting system. Once the primary path is established, it determines the most frequently suggested secondary route through a uniform convex procedure. Our results demonstrate the proposed method achieves significantly reduced computational costs and lower errors in the primary path, resulting in shorter overall travel times. Furthermore, we show the approach can be implemented with minimal memory requirements, making it suitable for real-time integration into connected vehicle systems.

In this study, we investigate the relationship between flat-minima optimizers and improved generalization capabilities in neural networks. We developed an innovative method to efficiently compare the generalization performance of neural networks optimized using stochastic gradient descent and those optimized using L2-regularized stochastic gradient descent. This method allowed us to perform a large-scale cross-sectional analysis of over 10,000 neural networks trained with different optimizers, learning rates, and data sizes. Our findings reveal that L2-regularized SGD consistently outperforms SGD in terms of generalization, even when flat-minima optimizers are not confirmed to be present. Furthermore, we formulated a novel metric to quantify the flatness of neural networks at test time and demonstrated that there is a positive correlation between this metric and generalization capabilities.

This study introduces a cutting-edge system that utilizes a non-linear frequency filtering technology to minimize unwanted electromagnetic emissions and prevent interference overload in wireless transmitters and receivers. The system consists of a unique frequency filter that mirrors an active nonlinear component, allowing it to cover the entire radio frequency spectrum and withstand extreme signal conditions without degrading the desired signal. Our experimental results show that this technology can block extremely powerful interference signals while allowing the desired signal to pass through, making it an effective means of separating signals with large intensity differences.

This study examines the dynamics of an infectious disease spreading across different regions, each with unique spatial, non-linear and dynamic characteristics, and interacts randomly with neighboring areas. We investigate the fundamental reproduction number, $\mathcal{R}_0$, and its impact on the disease's spread and prevalence in each region, and develop a statistical model to forecast the disease's future trajectory. This analysis is grounded in the SIS framework, and we investigate the disease's spread through both the disease-free equilibrium and its stability, and through numerical simulations to validate our findings.

We suggest combining word and phrase representations with context information and structural dependencies extracted from syntactic trees to enhance the accuracy of term-matching through a supervised approach using various neural network models.

We consider a scenario of random geometric graphs, G($n, r_{n}$), on $n$ points chosen randomly in a $d$-dimensional space. Each pair of points is connected by an edge with a probability of $r_{n}$, which represents the maximum distance between vertices. We investigate the $k^{th}$ order component number, denoted by $\eta_{k}(G)$, which is the number of connected components where each subgraph has a diameter of at least $k$ times the distance between any two other points in the graph. We establish that for a given $k$, the values $\eta_{k}(G)$ follow a Poisson distribution with a mean and variance of $\mu_{k}(n)$, which is determined by specific coefficients and $n$; these values converge to constants $k^{2}$, $k$, or 0 as $n$ is increased. Additionally, we prove that the cumulative distribution functions of $\eta_{k}(G)$ are the survival functions of the corresponding Poisson distributions. We further derive a central limit theorem for $\eta_{k}(G)$, which states that the random variable $\eta_{k}(G)$ is almost surely close to a normal random variable with a specific mean and variance. A novel approach is developed to calculate and visualize the three-dimensional equilibrium structures of rotating stars, which can possess arbitrary shapes and rotational velocities. This method employs a Lagrangian framework, where material elements are followed through time, and the star's non-rotating and rotating states are represented by two separate configurations. The equilibrium state is determined by minimizing the kinetic energy under given rotational constraints using a quasi-Newton minimization algorithm. Our approach is tested on simple cases, which confirms its accuracy and reliability, and also allows for the visualization of the star's material elements. This method is particularly useful for modeling the internal dynamics of isolated neutron stars, which are challenging to study using traditional Eulerian approaches. Our method is expected to be an essential tool for simulating the internal evolution of these neutron stars, which are often found in binary systems that can interact with other stars, supernovae, or black holes.

This paper explores the characteristics of an extended Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetime and establishes a key link between energy density and expansion rates, ultimately revealing that the resulting spacetime exhibits properties akin to those of a stable, gravitational system.

We investigate the generation and characterization of a special category of quantum systems - strongly nonlocal sets, consisting of many-partite quantum states. Our research involves identifying the specific patterns that emerge when an initial nonlocal set undergoes local operations and tracing out in quantum systems. To achieve this, we develop a framework that examines the properties of an underlying quantum code, represented by a linear map on a Hilbert space, and analyze how it behaves under specific quantum operations and state transformations. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the relationships between these quantum codes and nonlocal quantum systems.

To effectively analyze web user behavior, we've developed an algorithm capable of identifying users' intended destinations. This involves categorizing visited web pages and predicting users' attitudes towards each category based on their navigation habits. By incorporating users' complete browsing history, our algorithm can accurately predict their intentions. It works by training classifiers for each category to recognize users' typical behavior, such as frequent or infrequent visits. These classifiers are then used to predict visit intentions. Notably, our algorithm can also handle incomplete sequences and users' few visits to certain pages. In our experiments using a real-world dataset, the algorithm achieved high accuracy in predicting top destinations and intentions.

A novel reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) design is proposed for
downlink multiuser communication systems, enabling a transmitter to utilize an
RIS for signal reflection before transmission. The RIS features a transmissive type
configuration, allowing for the detection of channel state information (CSI) and
subsequent phase shifts for enhanced communication. The transmission strategy
involves a multi-phase approach: first, the RIS phase shift values are calculated
from CSI, then, the transmitter adjusts its transmit power based on RIS-aided CSI
and minimizes the overall power consumption. The proposed RIS-assisted transmission
strategy is formulated as a joint optimization problem to balance system
throughput, RIS phase shift values, and transmit power. The problem is then
solved using an iterative algorithm combining alternating direction method of
multipliers (ADMM) and bessel interpolation, providing a practical solution for
RIS-assisted communication systems, especially in scenarios where only RIS phase
shift values can be controlled. The simulation results demonstrate that the
proposed RIS-assisted transmission strategy can achieve significant improvements
in system throughput, with a maximum increase of 23.9 dB over a conventional
system without RIS.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) focuses on learning from pre-collected datasets
without requiring ongoing interactions with the environment. Conventional
offline RL methods typically rely on a specific distributional assumption or
require significant computational resources. This paper introduces an adaptive and
efficient offline RL algorithm that can function without such assumptions.
The proposed method utilizes a neural network to simultaneously represent Q and V
functions and relies on a novel contrastive loss, which encourages the Q function
to closely approximate the value function. By doing so, it can learn without
reliance on a specific distributional assumption. Empirical results demonstrate
that our algorithm outperforms existing offline RL methods across various
benchmarks.

We propose a novel type theory for higher-order programming, which enables polymorphic functions to be typed up front, with their running times determined afterwards. By adopting a constructive version of Martin-Löf's type theory, we can derive implicit free theorems through existential quantification. However, this approach comes with a catch: the theorems in question become invalid if we adopt a non-constructive approach. To mitigate this problem, we have identified a specific class of theorems that remains valid across different polymorphic interpretations, including those involving denotational semantics. These are known as beta-theorems, which can be derived from free theorems through various logical transformations. Our proposed type theory has been implemented within Agda, with the associated code available for review.

Our research involves observing the galaxy J0437+2456, which is a distant and isolated CIV lens system, using the Hubble Space Telescope. We collected and analyzed data from two different times, discovered a significant change in the system, and determined that a previously inactive lensing system has now become gravitationally active. We calculated the angular separation between the lens and the source to be approximately 2.25 mas. Based on the observed time delay, we were able to determine the speed at which the galaxy is moving outwards to be approximately 1900 ± 100 km/s. We also estimated the mass of the galaxy to be approximately 1.61 × 10^11 solar masses and its internal velocity dispersion to be approximately 240 ± 20 km/s. We calculated the acceleration due to gravity of the system to be approximately 1.04 ± 0.08 m/s^2 and its lensing potential to be approximately 0.23 ± 0.01. We also estimated the time of the next change in the system to be approximately 8.8 years. We also determined that a previously discovered time delay in the galaxy J0710+741 is caused by a cluster that the galaxy is a member of. We also discovered that a previously discovered time delay in the galaxy J1138+3130 is caused by a previously unknown lens.
