The increasing adoption of smart meters has made it possible to effectively detect electricity theft over communication networks. This paper presents a novel approach to electricity theft detection, utilizing a deep learning network that combines recurrent neural networks and an autoencoder to analyze smart meter data. The proposed system first extracts key features from time-series readings and filters out non-critical anomalies, including those caused by weather conditions. A deep recurrent neural network is then employed to identify and classify various types of anomalies, including electricity theft, at a high level of accuracy. The proposed method was evaluated using real smart grid data from a French utility company and demonstrated high performance in detecting electricity theft.

Our research focuses on understanding the characteristics of sparse and tight surface graphs, 
with an emphasis on constructing specific examples, like torus-based tight surfaces, 
and surface graphs arranged according to the lexicographic ordering, 
particularly for surfaces with three or more handles.

Researchers have successfully measured the lifetime of the $\Xi_{cc}^{++}$ baryon for the first time, using 37.6 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data collected at 13 TeV with the LHCb detector. The lifetime of the $\Xi_{cc}^{++}$ baryon was determined to be approximately 1.00 $\times$ 10$^{-15}$ seconds, with a 17 nanosecond statistical uncertainty and a 7 nanosecond systematic uncertainty. This finding aligns with theoretical expectations for the lifetime of charmed baryons.

This study introduces an unsupervised learning technique for remote sensing, called subspace clustering, which can discover underlying data structures without the need for labeled data. A novel approach, named Subspace Clustering via Non-matrix Block Alternating Descent (SC-NMBAD), has been proposed for remote sensing data. It utilizes a novel linear subspace model, which represents data as a linear combination of multiple subspaces, and employs non-matrix block alternating descent to optimize the model. A new regularization term, which incorporates the inter-relationship between different subspaces, is also proposed to enhance the model's performance. Theoretical convergence results have been established for the SC-NMBAD method. Experimental evaluations using real-world remote sensing data validate the superiority of the SC-NMBAD method over state-of-the-art approaches.

Arctic sea ice plays a vital role in Earth's climate system, with changes in its thickness and coverage having a profound impact on global processes. Accurate predictions of these changes rely on understanding the underlying factors influencing sea ice formation, and this paper investigates how variations in ocean temperature and heat flux influence the formation of Arctic sea ice. Using a coupled ice-ocean model, we simulated the effects of varying heat flux and ocean temperature on sea ice properties, and found that thermal conductivity and albedo are highly sensitive to ocean temperature and heat flux, respectively. We also discovered that ocean temperature has a greater impact on sea ice formation than heat flux at the ocean surface. Furthermore, we found that the vertical growth of sea ice has a greater influence than horizontal movement in setting the boundary conditions for ice temperature, and that ice thickness is primarily determined by ocean temperature rather than heat flux.

Our research demonstrates the creation of a final state selectively by employing a method called resonant dynamic Attractive-Repulsive Potential scattering (DRP) on ultracold atoms interacting with RbRb molecules. By utilizing a dynamic magnetic field, we can observe the atom-molecule scattering process and measure the final state's distribution. The method enables us to produce the $^85$Rb$_2$ molecule in its lowest energy state. The method's efficiency is further validated by measuring the momentum distribution of the produced molecules. By comparing the experimental findings with the predictions of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, we can confirm that the method is effective in producing the desired state. The method's potential in studying the interaction between atoms and molecules is further explored by discussing the DRP's generalization to the $^{87}$Rb$_2$ molecule and other molecular species.

A unified statistical framework has been developed, which incorporates the principles of nonextensive thermostatistics and superstatistics. This framework, built on superstatistic, a probability distribution of generalized Tsallis parameters, is found to be a natural extension of superstatistics. As a result, the framework's statistical properties are derived from those of its constituent probability distribution and Tsallis parameter distribution. These properties include mean, variance, and higher-order moments, as well as the superstatistic's response function and the distribution of generalized Tsallis parameters. Furthermore, the framework's behavior in the presence of external fields and the emergence of a generalized Pareto distribution are discussed.

We create a theoretical model of a Floquet state that combines characteristics of Weyl semimetal thin films and Weyl insulator systems. By using a two-dimensional Weyl Hamiltonian and a time-periodic potential, our model exhibits unique Weyl points in the Brillouin zone that change periodically with time, along with distinct Majorana cones in its Floquet spectrum. Unlike traditional Floquet Weyl semimetal states, these new states are topologically trivial and feature distinct band gaps. We explore the electronic properties of these gapless states through the lens of the semion bound state and the chiral edge mode, both of which display unusual behavior. Notably, the bound state exhibits a half-integer topological charge, while its associated chiral mode is uniquely responsive to the phase of the Floquet drive, displaying characteristics of chiral Floquet skyrmions.

As more individuals generate and consume computational resources, it becomes increasingly difficult for centralized systems to effectively manage distributed computing. In response, we've developed a decentralized computing protocol, referred to as the "Computing Share Economy". This protocol enables distributed computing and incentivizes participants to provide accurate computational services while maintaining the security and privacy of contributors. In our proposed scheme, participants can choose to either supply computational resources or utilize them, while a decentralized market mechanism aligns individual interests with overall system requirements. Incentivization mechanisms are implemented through a combination of correct computation rewards and system disruption penalties. Additionally, our protocol ensures secure access and confidentiality of computational resources and results. Through formal verification, we've confirmed the security and correctness of our protocol. In contrast to traditional approaches, our proposed protocol boasts a more decentralized structure, improved fault tolerance, enhanced computational efficiency, and increased market liquidity.

This research introduces a pioneering end-to-end framework for compressing 3D point clouds using rate-distortion optimization (RDO). A primary hurdle in this field is training the encoder and decoder simultaneously while incorporating RDO, which poses an insurmountable challenge due to the incompatibility of optimization and back-propagation. To address this, our proposed solution employs a novel cascaded compression method and develops an iterative optimization algorithm to evaluate the distortion metric. This allows our model to be trained end-to-end without any restrictions. Experiments on multiple benchmarks validate the efficiency of our proposed method in terms of performance-quality balance and distortion reduction.

The QCD phase diagrams for two colors to 3 colors have been mapped out by the Budapest-Wuppertal and Wuppertal-Princeton-Columbia-Satish Mathur collaborations through lattice simulations. A notable alignment between the lines marking the onset of chiral symmetry breaking and deconfinement transitions serves as evidence for a single critical point in these 4D systems. Furthermore, this coincidence suggests that a single critical point in these systems may also be present in systems with 4 colors or higher, potentially resolving long-standing debate.

The rapid expansion of deep learning in medical imaging has been hindered by the scarcity of labeled data, which necessitates extensive manual annotations. Despite the high cost and expertise needed for accurate labeling, researchers have developed self-supervised learning methods that utilize unsupervised data to achieve comparable results. Our study explores self-supervised learning for automatic liver tumor segmentation in CT images. We developed a Contrastive Learning framework, which uses a multi-scale feature encoder to identify invariant representations and a multi-head attention mechanism to preserve local details. Our method is evaluated on the MS-Tumor dataset and demonstrates superior performance over existing solutions, with a mean Dice coefficient of 0.87 and an average Hausdorff distance of 1.27 mm.

A significant drawback of traditional font creation methods involves substantial data annotation expenses and time. To mitigate this, we introduce a novel approach, few-shot font generation, which leverages limited information to generate a new font. This work presents a font synthesis framework that incorporates a font representation model, a font-style generator, and a font renderer. The framework is based on a novel style generator that utilizes a multi-view attention mechanism to effectively combine different font attributes. To optimize the model's performance, we propose a multi-view loss function and a semantic alignment method that accounts for character semantics. Experimental results on various tasks, including font style transfer, font style classification, and font retrieval, demonstrate the proposed approach's superiority over state-of-the-art techniques.

In the research, the metric formalism is used to examine how a charged fluid coupled to the torsion of spacetime affects a spherically symmetric, stationary environment with a non-uniform, isolated source. It was discovered that this interaction gives rise to the torsional analogues of the monopole analogues of the Hall effect and the magneto-Poynting effect. The study also found that in a non-matter context, the torsion-induced effects can be equivalent to a charged, rotating fluid's influence on its surroundings.

This paper presents an innovative method for optimizing video streaming using digital twins, especially designed for systems with varying battery life. The approach involves creating personalized models for each user based on their unique device characteristics, and then employing these models in an adaptive video streaming system powered by digital twins. The key challenge is to balance the computational costs associated with model creation and usage, while ensuring an optimal streaming performance. To address this issue, we propose a new algorithm, Cloud-DTAVS, which employs machine learning and multi-agent systems to dynamically adjust the quality of video streams according to each user's device performance. The design of Cloud-DTAVS includes a cloud-based system for constructing and utilizing user-specific models, a network of digital twins at the edge, and an adaptive control system for adjusting video stream qualities in real-time. The effectiveness of Cloud-DTAVS is demonstrated through simulations, which show that it significantly improves the user's streaming experience, especially in terms of quality and delay.

The observation of high-energy neutrinos by IceCube and AMANDA has led to a significant prediction that the flavor ratio of the neutrinos emitted by the cosmos is 1:1:1:0. This is based on the assumption that neutrinos oscillate, which is supported by experiments that have detected neutrino oscillations using artificial sources. This paper will discuss the theoretical background of the cosmic neutrino flux and the experimental evidence that has led to the prediction of the 1:1:1:0 ratio, as well as the challenges that must be addressed by future studies in order to verify this prediction through further experiments.

We establish the almost sure, global wellposedness of a periodic Schrödinger equation with various nonlinear components. Specifically, we prove the solvability of the equation under general cubic, quartic, quintic, and sixth-order nonlinear terms, provided the initial data belong to $L^2$. This result, combined with the known global wellposedness of the damped wave equation, allows us to obtain global wellposedness for an associated wave equation with these nonlinear components. Interestingly, the corresponding linear wave equation is ill-posed and has a finite lifespan, highlighting the significance of our results.

Human control of complex systems through networks relies heavily on high-throughput feedback communication. Advanced applications such as teleoperation and virtual reality benefit from tight sensor and actuator connections. However, high data rates often come at the cost of increased latency. Nevertheless, research indicates that latency within specific bounds can be tolerated by humans, necessitating the optimization of communication to achieve the highest possible throughput within acceptable latency constraints. In this paper, we introduce a novel method for optimizing data compression in real-time applications, initially tested in a teleoperation experiment and later extended to a broader testbed. The study reveals that our approach achieves substantial performance enhancements compared to traditional methods.

The central star cluster of the supernova remnant Sgr A East is suspected to be the future home of the compact star Sgr A*. The star cluster is located near the supermassive black hole Sgr A*. This research aims to determine the age of the star cluster in order to predict the current mass of Sgr A*. The cluster's age is estimated by analyzing the luminosities of main-sequence stars in the cluster using the Hubble Space Telescope's data. The analysis also takes into account the stars' spectral types and luminosities, which are then compared to theoretical models of stellar evolution. The results indicate that the cluster's age is around 40 million years, with a current mass for Sgr A* of approximately 2.1-4.2 times the mass of the sun.

A number of recent findings at the LHCb observatory have suggested that lepton universality might be broken in certain decays involving b-hadrons. To investigate this, a detailed analysis of semileptonic b-hadron decays to a c-quark and a W-boson is needed. The decay rates of different flavor combinations within this process should either be consistent with the Standard Model or provide clear evidence of non-Standard Model behavior. This paper reports on new measurements of the charge of the R-K* particle and the first assessment of electric charge for the R-K+ particle, both made possible by analyzing 1.0/fb of data collected at 7 TeV and 8 TeV energy levels. The findings show that measured values align with predictions made by the Standard Model.

This research presents a cutting-edge system for discourse segmentation and connective detection. The design incorporates several novel approaches, including the incorporation of manually designed features that have demonstrated superior performance in related NLP tasks. The study also introduces a new method for assigning connective arguments to specific discourse connectives, yielding more accurate results. The design further introduces a multi-task learning architecture that has been tested across various domains, resulting in notable improvements in F1 scores for both tasks. The proposed system was evaluated against recent state-of-the-art models in the field and achieved superior results.

The future of networks appears uncertain, with multiple promising technologies vying to shape the future internet's architecture and service offerings. Mobile Network Operators' primary concerns are adapting to these changes and capitalizing on the emerging opportunities. This text outlines key challenges, service creation, and usage factors for future networks, with a focus on the requirements and obstacles specific to each stage of the service delivery process.

The Okubo-Weiss criterion is reinterpreted using the geometric approach to the Euler equations. This geometric method views the Euler equations as a manifold's conformal curvature connections and yields an equivalent to the Okubo-Weiss criterion based on integrated geometric invariants. This connection provides a deeper understanding of the physical phenomena behind the mathematical results, linking geometric properties to physical properties like vorticity and the second invariant. Moreover, it's demonstrated that the geometric approach can be expressed through the helicity of the flow. This approach also offers a generalization of the Okubo-Weiss criterion to higher-dimensional spaces with corresponding definitions and generalizations of the 2-sphere.

Lee-Wick theories involve unusual particles called Lee-Wick partners, alongside the standard model particles. Excitations within these unusual particles may lead to undefined energies. Theoretical implications suggest these undefined energies could give rise to a unique form of gravitational interaction observable in the standard model framework. This work explores the potential of the Lee-Wick theory in explaining the Hubble constant's tension. It involves calculating how the Lee-Wick partners affect the cosmic microwave background radiation's power spectrum, particularly focusing on how their undefined energies give rise to a distinct form of gravitational interaction.

The objective of image style transfer is to convert the style of an image into another. Current neural style transfer methods primarily rely on adversarial losses to eliminate texture details from the content image while adopting the style of the target image. However, these methods face a significant challenge in retaining the full richness of the content's semantic information. To address this issue, we have developed a new self-supervised learning framework that enables style transfer by leveraging only the target image's semantic information. Our method involves creating a synthetic auxiliary image with the same semantic categories as the target image and then training an encoder-decoder network to generate this image. The network is also trained to predict the semantic categories of the target image. To enhance the quality and diversity of the synthesized images, we have designed an innovative auxiliary image generation method that involves combining the auxiliary image with the target image using a specific transformation matrix. The transformation matrix is learned through self-supervised learning using an auxiliary image generator. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method achieves higher quality and diversity in the generated content while maintaining its style.

We investigate the impact of geometric optimization on the dissipation that systems experience during thermodynamic processes. To do this, we use a specific model to analyze the thermodynamic transport properties of a one-dimensional classical particle system. We calculate the system's dissipation and resistance by comparing the actual current to the maximum current achievable, and we show that geometric optimization significantly reduces dissipation and leads to enhanced performance in thermodynamic tasks. Our findings are applicable to a broad range of thermodynamic systems.

The production of vector-like top partners at the LHC is investigated in detail. The decay of top partners occurs through two channels: one involving a Z boson and bottom quark, and another involving a Higgs boson and either a top or bottom quark. The current constraints from searches for top quark pairs are found to be relatively weak, whereas the same constraints are highly restrictive for W boson-associated production of top quarks. Upper limits are placed on the production cross-section of top and lightest vector-like top partners, which in turn restrict the parameter space of the model. The decay of top partners to Higgs bosons into light or bottom quarks is found to be a promising signal for the high-luminosity phase of the LHC, providing a more robust exclusion of the parameter space compared to direct searches for top and lightest vector-like top partners decaying into a top and a W boson.

This study examines the stability of two distinct fluids under the influence of complex acoustic fields. Fluid 1 is subjected to an incident sound wave modified by the properties of fluid 2, while fluid 2 is perturbed by the fields generated by fluid 1. Using the linearized Navier-Stokes equations and the KZK and linearized Euler equations, we derived the acoustic field equations for fluid 1. The linearized Euler equation for fluid 2 was then used to determine the acoustic field at the fluids' interface. By applying the normal modes theory, we determined the stability of the fluids. Our results show that the fluids are unstable when the acoustic fields are in phase, with phase differences of π leading to a reduction in instability. Our theoretical model was verified against a numerical simulation, with good agreement between the two methods.

Our research focuses on identifying specific reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces linked to holomorphic functions defined on a specified closed disk, $\overline{D}_r$. We provide an in-depth analysis of the Dirichlet space $\mathcal{D}(D_r)$ with respect to the normalized Mobius transformation mapping the unit disk to $D_r$, and demonstrate that it serves as a reproducing kernel Hilbert space in specific instances. Furthermore, we explore other reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces connected to $\mathcal{D}(D_r)$, including multipliers space of $\mathcal{D}(D_r)$ and its orthogonal complements within $\mathcal{D}(D_r)$.

The high-energy gamma-ray facility, ELI-Bland, is set to become the most powerful gamma-ray source in the world, emitting photons with energies reaching up to 10 DezMeV. The gamma-ray beam will be produced through electron bremsstrahlung in a solenoid channel. The target's position can be adjusted to achieve the desired beam size. The gamma radiation will interact with a variety of high-Z targets, leading to the emission of various particles, including alpha particles, heavier ions, and fragments. The gamma-ray source's energy spectrum will be influenced by the interaction with these emitted particles, necessitating a thorough understanding of the shift in energy. The aim of this study is to investigate the shift in energy of the emitted gamma-ray beam due to the interaction with these particles. The results of this research will be crucial for designing the gamma-ray channel accurately.

This research introduces a novel method for identifying events in text by combining two key concepts: the syntactic structure of sentences and the process of learning from labeled examples. Our approach involves creating a graph to represent the parts of a sentence in a hierarchical manner, and then using this graph to extract relevant information from the text. We have tested our method using two different datasets and two different types of text, and compared it to a straightforward approach that does not involve constructing a graph. Our results show that our method is more effective, and that it can be used to improve the performance of a related task called event trigger identification.

We examine a Bayesian approach to parameter estimation for discrete-time hidden Markov models, where the transition probabilities and observation probabilities are defined by the outputs of Gaussian mixtures. We demonstrate that the corresponding Markov chain has geometrically ergodic properties, enabling us to establish law of large numbers and central limit theorem results for the posterior distribution. Additionally, we provide an estimate for the rate of convergence in posterior convergence, supported by numerical examples that illustrate our theoretical findings.

We present a simplified approach to achieving complete quantum control over a system of multiple atomic nuclei in a two-dimensional arrangement, utilizing a limited number of laser beams to establish and maintain entanglement between them. Leveraging the unique properties of the atomic structure of the 87Y isotope, our method enables the creation of a quantum state from its two fundamental components. With our setup, it is possible to produce high-fidelity entangled states at will, paving the way for exploring quantum computing and the distribution of quantum key at the single-particle level.

Nonlinear dynamical systems with random noise have become a significant focus in multiple fields due to their relevance in modeling such systems. This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of the transfer operator, a fundamental concept in dynamical systems theory, in the context of Markov chains and Poincaré maps. Building upon these foundations, we develop a framework for linear response theory (LRT) in the presence of noise, adapting the ZGRT to Markov chains and Poincaré maps. Our research also explores the connections between LRT and the Mori-Zwanzig equations, as well as the implications of our approach for systems exhibiting hyperbolic behavior.

This study delves into wave propagation patterns in a one-dimensional medium that experiences linear and nonlinear energy loss.  A mathematical model is developed to capture the behavior of high-frequency waves in a thin, high-absorption regime.  By analyzing the limiting properties of this model as parameters for absorption loss and frequency increase tend towards their maximum values, our research reveals that this system yields solutions that transition smoothly from the well-known Korteweg-de Vries equation.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in explainable reinforcement learning (XRL) as a means of developing transparent and dependable learning agents. XRL's core goals involve creating algorithms that not only generate reliable policies but also provide users with a clear understanding of the decision-making process. This paper delves into the challenges of defining and measuring explainability within the context of RL. In particular, it examines and explains the decision-theoretic framework for RL explainability, highlighting its significance in the field of XRL. To facilitate a deeper understanding, it applies this framework to a well-known RL algorithm and uses a case study to visually illustrate the concept. Finally, the paper outlines a practical approach for designing explainable RL algorithms.

We investigate a fragment of the first-order $\mu$-calculus with a single variable, which corresponds to a combination of both classical and intuitionistic modal logics. Our systematic approach defines a sequence of modal calculi that align with the normal modal logics and their respective intuitionistic counterparts. These calculi incorporate a product operator, mirroring the traditional $\mu$-calculus operator, and enable us to establish a comprehensive framework for free models and cut-free sequent systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these calculi enjoy the property of strong admissibility, facilitating the straightforward design of these systems.

The signature of Gaussian processes with a wide range of Hurst parameters (0.25 to 1) can be uniquely identified by its signature, which is a specific probability measure that answers questions about the behavior and interactions of the process. This identification holds true even when the process has discontinuities, and our findings have significant implications for the tractability of the signature of the process. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the signature of fractional Brownian motion and the continuous part of fractional Brownian motion and the Riesz process are distinct from one another.

In 5G wireless cellular networks, angle-of-arrival (AOA) information is a crucial measurement for positioning user equipment, but it often comes with measurement errors. To mitigate these errors, a new method has been proposed that combines AOA measurements from base stations with least squares (LS) correction and those from non-line-of-sight base stations with Bayesian estimation. By incorporating the distribution of AOA errors, this method can accurately determine the user equipment's location and the cells it is connected to. Simulations have shown that it outperforms traditional methods that rely on minimum mean square error (MMSE) correction due to its sensitivity to the power delay profile of AOA errors. As an alternative, this method uses Bayesian estimation to account for this sensitivity and the non-line-of-sight nature of AOA measurements from certain base stations. As a result, it achieves lower localization error compared to traditional methods, and its accuracy is not significantly affected by the specific power delay profile of AOA errors.

We develop a method for examining the one-dimensional Bose gas with zero range interaction using a Bogoliubov transformation. This approach yields a key relationship between its thermodynamic properties and the Gross-Pitaevskii limit, established through a rigorous solution of the problem. This process involves a novel representation of the density matrix for a system in mixed states, derived from the Hilbert-Schmidt operator, along with a detailed analysis of the characteristics of the resulting kernel. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of the quantum deformed Bose gas, a model that deviates from the zero range interaction limit, with a focus on its thermodynamic properties and the establishment of the exact solution.

Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled significant progress in image inpainting tasks. However, a significant limitation of these methods remains their inability to handle resolution changes effectively. This issue arises because traditional image inpainting networks rely on pixel-level alignment based on input and target images, which becomes impractical when the resolution changes. To address this, we introduce a novel method that learns to align semantic features rather than pixel-level details, enabling seamless adaptation to images with different resolutions. This approach is demonstrated to be effective through experiments on multiple datasets for image inpainting and generation, showcasing its robustness in handling resolution changes.

This study introduces the stochastic Thresholding Bandit problem, focusing on two key types of shape constraints in reward functions: concave and convex. The aim is to find a near-optimal policy that maximizes rewards over time, despite limited information on function shape and unknown parameters. Two bandit problems are defined: the Concave Thresholding Bandit, where reward functions are concave, and the convex counterpart. Initially, a theoretical optimal solution is derived for the convex problem, followed by an algorithm providing a lower bound for all cases and an efficient solution for the concave problem.

We have discovered that NP and coNP are equivalent, specifically for determining the presence of a Hamiltonian cycle in a graph that does not already possess one. This was achieved through a reduction from a SAT problem. This discovery is unique because it stands in contrast to a well-known relationship between NP and coNP for general graphs.

We examine the evolution of hyperspheres within a higher-dimensional space and derive a relevant mean curvature formula. Subsequently, we investigate the long-term behavior of the constructed evolving hyperspheres.

In the context of the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, we examine the behavior of circular boundary conditions within the 2D XY model. By analyzing the energy and specific heat, we find power-law trends that align with expectations. Additionally, we investigate the correlation and susceptibility metrics, leading to the identification of critical exponents for which $\gamma$ and $\Delta$ values are approximately 1.307 and 2.01, respectively. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of vortex-like objects, known as vortons, in the model, including their characteristics and temperature-dependent densities. Our analysis shows that the average squared wavenumber of vortons increases in relation to the model's perimeter at temperatures below and above the critical temperature, indicating a discontinuous transition.

As artificial intelligence (AI) advances, it has sparked both positive and negative reactions from the public, necessitating a deeper understanding of the diverse attitudes towards AI. Our research analyzed over 1.3 million comments from the Chinese social media platform, Sina Weibo, where AI was mentioned, resulting in a dataset of 1,141,444 unique comments. Using a classification model, we categorized these comments as either supportive, neutral, or negative, providing insights into their overall public sentiment towards AI. Our analysis revealed a public sentiment score of 0.712, indicating a slight bias towards a negative attitude. Furthermore, we identified four primary themes in the public's perception of AI: concerns about job loss and ethics, benefits and applications of AI, trust and dependency on AI, and comparisons between AI and the internet. Our research findings offer valuable recommendations for promoting the development and use of AI, and potentially inspiring other countries to adopt similar strategies.

The $\Xi_c^0$ baryon, being unstable due to the strong interaction, breaks down primarily into a final state containing pions and kaons with the dominant decay mode driven by the $\Sigma_c^{(*)}$ baryon state. However, certain final states such as $\Xi_c^0 \to p K^- K^+$ have small branching fractions due to phase space limitations. This study examines the $\Xi_c^0 \to p K^-$ decay mode using the $\Lambda \to p \pi^-$ transition from the \emph{BESIII} experiment's full dataset, which includes $10.58$ fb$^{-1}$ of the \emph{Cornell}-\emph{Belle}-\emph{CLEO}-\emph{BABAR} (CB-EB) data, \emph{BELLE II} (EBS) and \emph{BESIII} (BE-EB) experiments. The results of this analysis are presented in the form of a branching fraction relative to the $\Xi_c^0 \to \Lambda \pi^-$ decay mode, along with the determination of the $\Xi_c^0 \to p K^-$ decay amplitude.

This study investigates the existence and distinctiveness of the fixed point for the product of two non-linear operators within the context of a Banach algebra. Moreover, it establishes a method of approximating the fixed point. As a demonstration of its utility, it applies these findings to a fractional differential equation with multiple delays, confirming the convergence criterion and distinctiveness of the solution.

We introduce a novel approach to actor-critic reinforcement learning, combining it with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. By leveraging HMC's ability to generate proposals near stable areas, our method enhances the policy parameter generator's exploration capabilities. In return, HMC benefits from the actor-critic approach by using policy gradients to define an energy function that indicates optimal solution locations. This collaboration yields more efficient exploration and, we claim, a more stable and efficient policy optimization method. In our experiments, this actor-critic-HMC method demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on several challenging continuous control tasks.

We investigate the quantum phase transitions within the extended Hubbard model on a triangular lattice. Our analysis reveals the emergence of a three-order transition from an antiferromagnetic state to a charge density wave (CDW) state, accompanied by a spin liquid phase in between. This transition between the AFM and CDW phases exhibits tricritical points, while the CDW phase is found to host two additional tricritical points. Notably, these tricritical points define the boundaries between the CDW, spin liquid, and charge ordered phases. Our investigation also uncovers a spin liquid phase characterized by a U(1) × U(1) symmetry and a vanishing order parameter of the CDW state, along with a spin liquid phase characterized by a U(1) symmetry. Our analysis of the CDW order parameter further shows that the spin liquid phase is separated from the CDW phase by a first-order transition at a specific filling of three electrons per site, while the spin liquid phase is separated from the charge ordered state through a first-order transition at a different filling of three electrons per site.

In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), effective use of environmental and inter-agent information is crucial. Although coordination knowledge has been shown to improve MARL efficiency, existing methods have limitations in utilizing coordination information, especially when agents are in close proximity. A novel method, the Semantics-aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework (S-MARL), has been proposed to address this issue by explicitly modeling the location and role of other agents in the environment, thereby enabling the agent to learn distinct representations for each agent and improve coordination, achieve higher rewards, in environments where agents are in close proximity. S-MARL's effectiveness has been demonstrated through experiments in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) in multiple scenarios.

To achieve efficient and robust locomotion, particle robots can be designed to move collectively, as this approach allows them to explore a wider range of motion while operating at lower power levels. A novel control method for collective locomotion is presented in this paper, utilizing a decentralized real-time algorithm that simulates the movement of each robot's neighbor. This control method is evaluated through both numerical simulations and experiments, demonstrating its ability to maintain a steady, high-speed locomotion despite disturbances and variations in density. Furthermore, the effects of initial density and disturbance on the particle system's stability are also investigated.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the atmospheric composition of the exoplanet WASP-31b, a hot Jupiter, by utilizing a combination of high-resolution spectroscopic data from the HARPS GTO program and a range of atmospheric models. The results indicate that the atmospheric conditions of WASP-31b are consistent with those of a typical hot Jupiter, with the presence of a high concentration of metals at its surface. The analysis also suggests that the planet's atmospheric temperature is relatively low, with a temperature gradient consistent with expected heat transfer mechanisms. The absence of detectable sodium and potassium in the planet's spectrum can be attributed to the effects of high atmospheric pressure and non-thermal chemical processes. The analysis also reveals that the planet's atmospheric conditions are similar to those of other hot Jupiters, such as HD 18977b and WASP-12b, and offer a possible explanation for the lack of sodium in WASP-12b's atmosphere. The results also offer insights into the atmospheric conditions of HD 18977b and suggest that the planet may have experienced a range of evolutionary phases, including a possible transition from a lower mass state. The analysis also indicates that the planet's atmospheric conditions are consistent with expected levels of metallicity, and that the planet may have experienced a range of evolutionary phases, including a possible transition from a lower mass state. High-performance computing applications often require substantial memory capacity, particularly in simulations that generate large data sets. However, storage challenges arise when these data sets are stored, necessitating a need for high-performance storage systems. This paper explores the feasibility of leveraging Non-Volatile RAM (NVRAM) to accelerate the backup process of significant data sets, resulting in considerable performance enhancements when compared to traditional RAM paired with high-performance storage systems.

Recent advancements in contrastive self-supervised learning have led to the development of effective models for identifying diverse visual concepts. However, the effectiveness of this approach in classifying functional magnetic mapping (fMRI) classification, particularly under conditions of small medical datasets, remains to be fully understood. This study investigates the potential of contrastive self-supervised learning for fMRI classification, introducing a novel approach that involves a self-supervised contrastive encoder and a supervised transformer decoder. By leveraging this encoder to extract key features and incorporating contrastive loss to enhance generalization, the approach demonstrates superior performance in fMRI classification tasks on multiple datasets, including the Cambridge Well-being, 1PPiT, and Hmax datasets.
We provide an explicit and straightforward proof that the signature modulo 8 of any bilinear form over a finite field is always congruent to 8 modulo 16.

For the first time, researchers have observed Cherenkov radiation from beryllium. By analyzing data from a particle accelerator, they examined a specific type of interaction involving an electron beam, a target, and the emission of a single photon with high energy. The collected information was used to set limits on the interaction between photons and beryllium, which is based on theoretical frameworks of new physics. The observed limits are more stringent than previously reported limits, with some being more than ten times stronger. The findings also include new restrictions on the interaction between positrons and nuclei.

This research paper introduces a novel method to automatically identify implicit arguments in sentences. Our approach has been tested on a large dataset containing several text types and argument link types, specifically for the energy argumentation context. The proposed method employs a combination of neural networks to classify implicit argument roles and to predict the co-occurrence of these roles in text. The first stage of the method employs a model that predicts the co-occurrence of two implicit argument roles in a sentence, and the second stage employs a model that classifies a specific implicit argument role in a given sentence. The implicit argument role is represented as a vector, which is calculated by combining the vector representations of two text segments representing the argument and its context. The performance of the proposed method is compared to that of a baseline model that relies on a machine learning classifier, and the results show that the proposed method achieves a higher accuracy.

In medical imaging diagnosis, the task of detecting abnormalities is critical but often overlooked by conventional loss functions which only focus on healthy tissue appearance. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel approach that combines a multi-task deep learning model with a unique loss function. Our proposed loss function penalizes model predictions when large differences occur between predicted and actual tissue states in healthy areas, and we validate its effectiveness through experiments on four large public image datasets, with impressive results showing a significant average improvement of 2.0-4.0% in comparison to widely used loss functions over multiple iterations.

The AIC is a widely used statistical tool for model selection, but its application in Gaussian process models is computationally intensive and often impractical.  A new method has been developed that efficiently calculates AIC values in GP regression by approximating the log marginal likelihood.  This approach, based on Laplace approximation, has been shown to produce results comparable to a more complex method, but at a significant speed increase, up to 1000 times faster.  By integrating this method, a new package called gp-aic is now available for use, providing researchers with a user-friendly tool for AIC calculations in GP models.

Our research confirms that the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence contains a vast number of distinct binary patterns of any specified length. However, exceptions to this vast number do exist, examples of which we have computationally discovered. Moreover, our research indicates that the probability of an arbitrary binary pattern of length n occurring in the sequence approaches 2/3 as n becomes increasingly large.

The dynamic classifier selection issue is explored, focusing on a scenario with a set of trained classifiers available. The goal is to determine the best classifier for a given input among the set, enhancing overall performance and exactly predicting a minority of misclassified instances in the training data. A method called LADACS is introduced, utilizing a low-rank matrix approximation to facilitate the search for hard-to-predict instances. A new loss function called log-likelihood loss function is developed to identify difficult instances. Furthermore, a dynamic classifier selection algorithm called LADACS is proposed, leveraging low-rank matrix approximation and the log-likelihood loss function. The effectiveness of LADACS is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets.

The Tianlai project is a radio cosmological survey that uses 21cm intensity mapping to explore the dark energy phenomenon. This involves constructing a vast network of antennas across a wide area. The first phase, consisting of 40,000 antennas, is focused on detecting the dark energy by mapping large scales. This article provides an overview of the first facility, known as Tianlai 40K, which is situated in a remote location in China and offers a unique environment for the project. The article also describes the strategies for data transmission and processing from multiple stations to a central site. This processing will be done using a cloud-based system that is being developed and tested with a small-scale test network of 10 antennas. The test network successfully achieved the required data transmission speed, and the development of the full data processing pipeline is underway. This pipeline will be used to process the full dataset, allowing researchers to refine their understanding of dark energy.

A quantum device utilizing the unidirectional propagation of spin waves can be a highly efficient qubit for quantum processing. Achieving this requires materials that exhibit spin superfluid properties under certain conditions, which include low spin-wave scattering and slow magnon group velocities. We have investigated the magnon modes in a highly correlated electronic system, specifically a half-doped cuprate superconductor. Our findings show that half-doped cuprates possess a spin superfluid state, which is characterized by significant spin-wave scattering and slow magnon velocities. This unique combination of properties in half-doped cuprates makes them potential candidates for creating efficient spin-based processing devices.
This paper provides definitions and criteria for the strict positive definiteness of the Fredholm integral operator in the context of metric spaces.

A subset within the set of nonnegative real numbers that is closed under addition is termed a positive monoid. This concept is applied to the set of continuous linear functionals on the space of polynomials of a real number, denoted by $\mathcal P_n$, to explore its properties and characterize its elements. A generalization of these findings is also presented for continuous linear functionals on any weighted $n$-dimensional polynomial space.

To assess whether a potential risk management strategy is effective, we develop a statistical framework that considers an intervention's effectiveness when a treatment results in reduced disease incidence. The proposed method calculates the fraction of cases attributable to exposure, under different assumptions about risk in the exposed and non-exposed groups. We apply this approach to atypical prion diseases affecting humans and use genetic data to determine how a specific genetic mutation contributes to the risk of scrapie. The framework's versatility is demonstrated through various simulations and applications.
We extend Bloch's formula for the Chow groups of 0-cycles on schemes with dihedral singularities.

The study of particle production in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) LHCb experiment has revealed distinct characteristics in the production of ground state and excited charmonia particles. An investigation into how the production cross section ratios of excited charmonia and their ground state counterparts change with increasing particle multiplicity showed that for certain mesons like the chi2(nS) and psi(2S), their ratios decrease as events become more densely populated. Conversely, the ratios for other mesons like the chi_c(2D) and psi(2P) remain relatively consistent as the event density increases, suggesting that the initial stages of particle formation dominate their production processes.

We investigate the thermal conductivity properties of a quantum dot paired with electron and phonon energy reservoirs, connected through a perfect circuit. In the Kondo regime, thermal conductivity is analyzed in relation to specific, high-frequency (ω > D) and low-frequency (ω < D), energy ranges. High-frequency thermal conductivity is associated with spin excitations, while low-frequency conductivity is influenced by Kondo singlet formation, allowing for the transfer of spin entropy to heat. A dual description of this thermal conductivity is presented, with one approach focusing on spin and phonon fluctuations and the other on Kondo resonance and spin flip excitations. In the high-frequency range, thermal conductivity is found to be proportional to the square of the quantum dot's conductance, while in the low-frequency range, this relationship is linear. Experiments measuring thermal conductivity at both high and low frequencies can provide a comprehensive understanding of the quantum dot's energy levels and spin dynamics, ultimately allowing for the determination of the quantum dot's charge and spin energy gaps.

Given a polynomial $p$, we consider points $z_0$ close to its zeros and of modulus greater than $k$ times its minimum distance to the set of zeros. We analyze a specific modulus $\rho$ of $p$ near $z_0$ and of angle $\theta$ near $k\pi$. We find that the modulus $\rho$ is bounded by a specific limit near $z_0$ and of angle $\theta$ near $k\pi$. This limit is expressed as the product of the modulus of $z_0$ and a specific minimum distance to the set of zeros, multiplied by a specific constant. This result is applicable to entire functions $f$ of bounded distortion and a specific class of functions $f$ with normal singularities.

The dynamic behavior of bright solitons in a Bose-Einstein condensate, governed by the vector nonlinearity of the BEC, is investigated in the presence of dipole-dipole interactions. The attractive nature of these interactions is shown to significantly impact the solitons' stability, particularly when they are highly polarized. The introduction of DDIs is found to reduce the soliton's instability growth rate, leading to increased stability, and in some cases, by adjusting the strength of DDIs, unstable solitons can be transformed into stable ones.

We present a novel GM-MADOR algorithm, which is a mean-based derivative-free optimization technique that utilizes the geometric-arithmetic mean inequality to create a new family of multi-objective test functions. By leveraging this new approach, we demonstrate the effectiveness of GM-MADOR in outperforming other prominent optimization methods, including CMA-ES, on a range of benchmark functions.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the Teichmüller space for 3-manifolds, building upon the foundational work of  Morris, Pardon, and many others. Our primary focus lies in establishing a mapping class group action on this Teichmüller space, particularly when the 3-manifold in question has a torus boundary component. This is an advanced topic typically explored in graduate-level courses, which is why we have included a detailed, self-sufficient explanation of the necessary background material.

Creating realistic virtual avatars for communication is a complex task, requiring both 2D image analysis and 3D representation to capture an individual's appearance, expressions, and movements. Current methods rely on extensive 3D scanning or 2D video capture, resulting in either expensive equipment requirements or limited access to personal data. In contrast, methods utilizing a single RGB-D camera are expensive and often struggle with poor image quality. This research presents a new, cost-effective approach to generating personalized avatars from in-home RGB-D video recordings alone. By leveraging a neural network that combines 2D and 3D information, the system creates accurate 3D models and precise, natural-looking facial expressions. Additionally, the network's inherent symmetry property enhances face shape and pose capture. This novel approach offers a solution for creating highly realistic avatars, enabling users to communicate authentically and interactively within virtual environments.

Reconstructing a 3D face model from a single image is a challenging task due to variations in pose, lighting, and occlusions. Most current methods rely on sparse image correspondences and can be heavily affected by occlusions. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages dense semantic information extracted from images by vision transformers. By utilizing these features, our method can synthesize 3D facial geometry and texture information. By incorporating a 3D face shape model, our approach can accurately reconstruct 3D facial surfaces even in cases of partial occlusions. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in handling partial occlusions.

The challenge of balancing exploration and exploitation in Reinforcement Learning is a well-documented issue.
To overcome this problem, researchers have developed numerous techniques, including various adaptation methods for adjusting learning parameters based on the estimated uncertainty of actions.
However, these approaches often require complex computations to estimate action uncertainty or to balance exploration and exploitation, leading to inefficient or suboptimal performance in certain situations.
To address this issue, we introduce a simple and efficient method, the Gaussian Mixture Policy, which uses a mixture of Gaussian distributions as its underlying model.
This approach enables the direct use of well-established Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) algorithms for parameter estimation, allowing for the simultaneous generation of new actions and the estimation of action uncertainty, leading to improved learning efficiency and performance.

In this study, we introduce a novel policy gradient theorem within the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) that takes into account decentralized action selection. By adopting a localized perspective, this approach can efficiently handle vast and intricate MARL environments consisting of numerous agents and actions. The proposed theorem builds upon the multi-agent chain rule for policy gradients and offers a more stable and reliable solution by considering only the immediate gradient projection of each agent. The theoretical foundation of this theorem is supported by proof of convergence and a convergence rate estimate. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through empirical testing on both small and large MARL tasks, showcasing its ability to outperform existing methods significantly.

Researchers have conducted a study on the creation of two leading jets in proton-proton collisions, with a specific energy level of 0.8 TeV per collision and an inclusive jet energy range of 15 to 60 GeV. They utilized the CMS detector at the LHC to collect the data. Two within-jet axes were chosen for each event, and pairs of jets were formed based on these axes. To identify the leading and subleading axes, the minimum angle was used. A rapidity gap was observed to be significantly more likely to occur in pairs of jets that share the same leading jet angle. This finding is consistent with predictions from models that describe the interaction of gluons and the suppression of particles in hadron collisions.

Utilizing the Boltzmann Transport Theory, our analysis reveals that penta-silicene's unique electronic structure, characterized by distinct anisotropy and band degeneracy, significantly enhances its thermoelectric properties at room temperature. This is a rare occurrence in 2D materials, with one notable exception being MoS2. Penta-silicene's high thermoelectric performance is attributed to its exceptionally high electrical conductivity along the armchair mode and minimal thermal conductivity. Consequently, penta-silicene's figure of merit is remarkably high, reaching values of greater than 6 at room temperature for both n- and p-type configurations. Notably, these values surpass those of other 2D materials, including graphene and 1T-TiS2, and even those of bulk materials.

This research is further supported by a study of how the medium's energy density and temperature impact the formation of bound states within a hot, magnetized environment that includes both massive, strong and weak interactions. This study is based on a model developed by Zhu, in which scalar and vector interactions are represented by a combination of a scalar and a vector field that has a mass. Our results show that the binding energies of charmonium and bottomonium states decrease as the temperature and energy density of the environment increase. The LUXE experiment at DESY will conduct the most sensitive electron-proton dark matter interaction search to date, leveraging a novel approach. By injecting electron beams into a high-intensity interaction regime in a powerful laser wakefield accelerator, LUXE will utilize the unique physics of Bethe-Heitler pair production to detect dark matter interactions. This process will be sensitive to electron-nucleon cross-section interactions across a broad range of DM masses, from a few MeV to several TeV.

In various settings, such as logistics, government, and finance, there are scenarios where a defender is tasked with safeguarding limited, high-value resources like merchandise, data, or equipment against attacker strategies. This research introduces a new class of games called Green Security Games, which enable defenders to allocate limited patrols to protect valuable resources while encouraging vigilant citizen behavior. By integrating resource conservation and security measures, these games promote a collaborative approach to protection, aligning with the goals of companies and governments. This study presents a computational method for solving Green Security Games and examines its complexity, efficiency, and performance. Our analysis compares the outcomes of green and traditional protection policies and highlights the benefits of a collaborative approach, both through theoretical studies and simulations of real-world scenarios.

A cutting-edge approach to robot navigation in complex environments with uneven terrain is presented, utilizing deep learning and a novel attention mask algorithm to enhance terrain classification. This algorithm combines elevation and normal maps from 3D point cloud data with surface normal vectors to identify regions suitable for wheel rotation and safe wheel advance. The developed system, combining a deep neural network with the proposed terrain attention technique, has been successfully tested on an unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) during a 10-month field trial.

The statistical mechanics of a magnetic Ising model with uniaxial anisotropy confined to a triangular lattice is examined. The statistical mechanics of this model is influenced by a set of disorder parameters, which measure the magnitude of uniaxial anisotropy and frustration present in the system. The set of disorder parameters can be estimated from the disorder parameters of a different magnetic system, specifically the biaxial uniaxial Ising model, using a mathematical transformation that maps the latter to the former. This transformation is derived from the correspondence between the two models, and it is used to study the phase diagram of the uniaxial uniaxial Ising model. The results of this study are compared to those obtained from a numerical method called Monte Carlo simulations, applied to both models, and the comparison shows a strong agreement between the results. The comparison also reveals that the uniaxial uniaxial Ising model has a phase diagram that is similar to that of the biaxial uniaxial Ising model, and that both models exhibit the same types of phase transitions.

This study provides a comprehensive characterization of the generalized polarization tensors (GPTs) for planar conductivity inclusions with any number of connected, simply-shaped domains. By simplifying the multi-dimensional problem into a 1D boundary value problem, it addresses the GPTs through a linear eigenvalue analysis in the spectral domain. A novel, dimension-reducing approach is introduced, transforming the GPTs into a set of boundary-to-state operators, which are further defined by their frequency-dependent transfer matrices. This work's results are showcased through numerical examples that confirm the theory and highlight potential applications in the analysis of microelectronic devices.

Numerical simulations have revealed that stars with twisted and irregular magnetic fields develop local instabilities near their surface. This is particularly true for the $\ell=2$ azimuthal mode in simulations of star models with twisted magnetic fields and a coronal loop configuration. This mode of instability is strongly linked to the star's surface temperature variations, which are caused by its magnetic field. This is a departure from convective instability, which is typically the cause of instability in stars. This new type of instability has significant implications for the study of variable stars, particularly those with unusual magnetic properties. This could potentially lead to a new way to determine the magnetic properties of these stars.

This study examines the relationship between geometry and synchronization in networks, specifically in the context of simplicial complexes. We explore the role of spectral dimension in influencing the synchronization patterns of networks, inspired by recent findings on the spatial arrangement and synchronization of real-world networks. Building on this discovery, we develop a theory that explains how the spectral dimension of simplicical complexes impacts the synchronization of their nodes. We propose a novel approach to determine the spectral dimension of such networks and demonstrate that it is closely linked to the size and structure of their clique complex, allowing us to establish theoretical bounds on the spectral dimension of simplicial complexes. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations on synthetic and real-world networks.

High-performance libraries for sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) and linear solvers play crucial roles in various scientific and engineering applications, but they are often hindered by suboptimal performance on emerging accelerators like FPGas and custom chips. The development of optimized design flows is necessary to overcome this hurdle, but existing flows based on high-level programming languages are not well-suited for low-level accelerator programming. To address this challenge, we present a new design flow centered around the Hardware Design Language (HDL) to efficiently generate hardware accelerators for SpMV and linear solvers. Our HDL framework offers superior performance on diverse accelerators and outperforms existing HLS-based approaches in key areas.

Suppose F is a family of meromorphic functions in a domain D, G is a normal family consisting of non-constant limit functions, F and G share points partially in D, and f is any limit function of G. We prove that there exists a constant 0 < a < 1 such that the family {f(z) / (1 - z^k)} converges in probability to a non-constant holomorphic function at infinity for all z in an infinite subset of positive lower density in D, where k is a non-zero integer representing the period of F. This result generalizes a previous finding by Liu, Yang, and Zhang to more general settings and provides a partial solution to a problem posed by Hayman.

Human and robot teams can achieve their goals more efficiently by sharing knowledge and providing mutual assistance. However, without a shared mental representation of the task at various levels, human and robot teams are prone to confusion and errors. This study examines how individuals and groups coordinate and share their understanding of the task through communication. We discovered that two key factors contribute to effective teamwork: (1) intent sharing, where team members understand and align on the underlying goals and intentions, and (2) relevant information sharing, where team members exchange and utilize pertinent details to complete the task. We designed an experiment to investigate intent sharing and relevant information sharing in human groups working together. We found that human groups exhibit two distinct communication patterns: (1) parallel communication, where team members discuss the task's goals and intentions simultaneously, and (2) causal communication, where the exchange of relevant information depends on the shared understanding of the task's goals and intentions. This study provides insights into how humans coordinate their understanding of the task through communication, which can inform the development of more efficient human-robot teams.

We establish a category of higher-order bi-decomposable systems of Monge-Ampère type, whose Lagrangian pairs are associated with a specific type of Legendre transform, thereby linking them to certain types of Legendre convex functions. We prove a local Lagrangian structural stability result for Lagrangian pairs in this system, and show that they are semi-tubular. We also demonstrate that in a specific limiting case, these Lagrangian pairs correspond to a specific type of Legendre convex function, and that they are structurally stable in a global sense.

The electrolysis of hydrogen oxide solutions is a method for producing hydrogen and oxygen.  The process involves a sub-stoichiometric oxide layer that forms on the metal anode.  As a result, oxygen bubbles develop on the metal surface.  The growth and disappearance of these bubbles significantly affect the current density.  Theoretical models have been developed to study the movement of charge and matter through the bubble layer.  A new mathematical equation has been proposed to describe the movement of ions in the bubble region behind the oxide layer.  The bubble spacing and size are found to have a significant influence on the bubble expansion and contraction rates.  The research results are compared with existing experimental data.  The study also examines the impact of bubble spacing and size on the expansion and contraction rates.  Theoretical predictions indicate that oxygen bubble expansion slows down when the bubble is fully saturated with gas.  The slowdown is caused by a decrease in the rate of solubility of oxygen in the liquid.  The study also finds that the contraction rate of the bubble is faster than its expansion rate due to a decrease in the rate of solubility of water.  Theoretical models have been used to study the effect of bubble size on the contraction rate.  The research findings indicate that the bubble surface area decreases as it contracts. A study investigating the creation of particles that decay into pairs of muons is conducted. These particles are produced through high-energy proton collisions at 13 TeV and are analyzed in two discrete segments of the Large Hadron Collider's detector. A specific analysis technique allows the distinction between particles with long lifetimes and those with short ones, based on the difference in distance traveled before decay. By examining 2.3 fb^-1 of collected data from the Ultimate Muon System, an upper limit is set for the production rate of certain J/psi particles with increased lifetime.

We investigate the Dirac equation in a specific semimetal structure with varying electric and magnetic fields, represented by $p \cdot A(p)$, where $p$ is the momentum and $A$ the vector potential. This framework encompasses both a Dirac semimetal and a Weyl semimetal by adjusting their respective parameters. At high energies, the semimetal's parameters can be precisely defined from the band structure. At low energies, the semimetal's parameters are determined by their Fermi surface properties. This leads to a general power-law scaling, which bridges these two energy regimes. This scaling is verified for a second-order Dirac semimetal and a Weyl semimetal with a specific Fermi surface. This scaling is also used to establish a correlation between the semimetal's parameters and the conductivity tensor, which is essential for an unbiased classification of these materials.

Designing efficient concurrent data structures is a complex task that's simplified by using common sense. This research introduces a new approach to designing concurrent data structures by breaking them down into smaller components and using common sense to ensure correctness. Our method involves defining and verifying the safety properties of each component using a temporal logic framework, which is then translated into executable code. This enables us to verify the overall correctness of the design using a top-down topological ordering of its components. Our method was tested on a range of examples, including a search-and-insert data structure, and demonstrated its effectiveness.

We have successfully demonstrated the lifting of neodymium ferromagnets in a series of superconducting magnetic containers. Utilizing the Meissner effect allowed us to create the necessary conditions for levitation, which was then refined by precisely controlling the magnetic field generated by the neodymium magnets. As a result, the levitated magnets could be guided in a controlled manner through a series of superconducting barriers, a feat that has been previously achieved using much smaller superconducting bodies.

A search for ethynyl benzene (C3H3) was conducted in a collection of high-resolution spectra obtained from the Submillimeter Array towards the Orion Bar. Spectra from the (202-0) rotational transition were analyzed and no signals were detected, resulting in a 3-sigma upper limit of 0.7 K. This limit translates to a column density of 1x10^11 cm^-2. Notably, this search did not identify ethynyl benzene, but surprisingly revealed an unexpected emission line corresponding to a specific transition of a molecule known as ethynyl benzene. Initially, this was attributed to an unknown transition, but it was later confirmed to be an actual transition of the ethynyl benzene molecule. The analysis also provided an estimated column density of 1x10^12 cm^-2 and a kinetic temperature of 85 K for this molecule.

Our investigation focuses on the potential of using gravitational waves to test and distinguish between various asymmetric dark matter models, specifically the misalignment mechanism and the WIMP model, both of which are capable of creating a gravitational wave signal at the same time as the matter-antimatter imbalance. A notable difference between the two models is their predicted scale invariance; the misalignment mechanism typically lacks this characteristic, making it a more flexible theoretical framework when compared to the standard inert dark matter model. We examine the potential of future gravitational wave detectors, including the Cosmic Explorer, in detecting these unique features of asymmetric dark matter models, and we demonstrate how a future network of ground-based detectors could be used to pinpoint the primary source of a binary black hole merger event.

Using 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at 13 TeV by the ATLAS experiment at the LHC in 2015-2016, the $t\bar{t}Z$ cross-section in the 4-lepton channel has been determined. The cross-section in the 4-lepton channel is found to be 130.9$^{0.9}_{11.3}$ fb and including other channels the combined cross-section is found to be 130.5$^{3.8}_{8.4}$ fb. These results are in agreement with the Standard Model prediction.

We classify orbits of rebits in the action of the group $\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})^4$ on the four-dimensional manifold $\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})^4/\text{Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})^4$, where rebits are represented by specific types of matrices. This classification involves finding all possible combinations of non-zero rebit matrices, which are denoted as $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} a_1 & c_1 \\ c_2 & a_2 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} a_3 & c_3 \\ c_4 & a_4 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} a_1 & a_3 & 0 \\ 0 & a_2 & c_2 \\ 0 & 0 & a_4 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} a_1 & a_3 & c_1 \\ a_4 & a_{34} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & a_2 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, and determining the orbits they define.
